    Introduction

    OrgEverywhere brings Org mode to Sublime Text: the outline, todo states, dates, tables with formulas, source blocks, links and exporting of the org file you are editing, plus the agenda, capture, refile, clocking and everything else that works across all of your org files.

    Org is two things that are easy to mistake for one:

    1. Org files: a plain text markup, like markdown, for notes, lists, tables, code and documents.
    2. Org mode: the tools that work over a collection of those files - a todo list built from every file, an agenda of what is due, capturing a thought from anywhere into the right place, time tracking, exporting.

    Org can be a personal wiki, a notebook, a task manager, a time sheet, a literate programming notebook or a way of writing books. You do not need all of it to use any of it: start with headings and todo states and add the rest when you need it.

    OrgEverywhere and the orgs server

    Since 2.0 OrgEverywhere does the second half - everything that works across files - through the orgs server.

    orgs is a small server that keeps your org files parsed and answers questions about them: which files are org files, what is on the agenda today, where the heading with this id is, what links here, where a capture goes. Sublime, VSCode, the orgs command line, the worg web page and your phone all ask the same server, so they all see the same thing at the same moment. A clock started in Sublime is running in the browser.

    The file you are editing is still Sublime's: folding, todo cycling, tables, source blocks and the rest work on the buffer as you type, unsaved changes and all. Only questions about your other files go to the server, and the server reads what is saved.

    Without a server the editing half works as before; the agenda, refile, id links and the other cross file features say that the server is not connected.

    See Getting Started to install OrgEverywhere and connect it to orgs.

    How this manual is organised

    • Getting Started: installing, connecting to orgs, the keys.
    • Editing: headings, folding, navigation, lists, properties, dates.
    • Planning: todo states, the agenda, capture, refile, clocking, day pages.
    • Links: links, ids, backlinks and images.
    • Tables: tables, formulas, plots, the column view, dynamic blocks.
    • Source Blocks: running code, diagrams and tangling.
    • Exporting: html, latex, pandoc, reveal.js and the server's exporters.
    • orgs Server: what the server adds - query search and the query language, habits, clock reports, full text search and more.
    • Reference: every command and every setting, written beside the code that implements it.

    Further reading

    Getting Started

    Installing OrgEverywhere, connecting it to the orgs server, the keys and where settings live.

    Installing OrgEverywhere

    What you need

    • Sublime Text 4. OrgEverywhere runs on Sublime's python 3.8 plugin host (the package carries a .python-version file that asks for it), which Sublime Text 3 does not have.
    • Package Control, even for a manual install: it installs the python libraries OrgEverywhere uses and two helper packages.
    • An orgs server for everything that works across files (the agenda, capture, refile, clocking, id links…). Editing a file works without one. See Connecting to orgs.

    Installing with Package Control

    1. Open the command palette (ctrl+shift+p, cmd+shift+p on macOS) and run Package Control: Install Package.
    2. Pick OrgEverywhere.
    3. Restart Sublime once the libraries have installed.

    On its first start OrgEverywhere asks Package Control for two more packages if they are missing:

    • Table Editor: the table editing keys (moving between cells, inserting and deleting rows and columns) are Table Editor's commands.
    • PowerShell: syntax highlighting for powershell source blocks.

    It also copies its settings into Packages/User/OrgEverywhere.sublime-settings the first time it runs (see Settings).

    Installing by hand

    To run from a git checkout, clone the repository into Sublime's Packages folder under the name OrgEverywhere. The name and its case matter: the python modules import each other as OrgEverywhere.something, so a folder called orgeverywhere or OrgEverywhere-master does not load.

    Preferences > Browse Packages… opens the right folder. From a terminal:

    # macOS
git clone https://github.com/ihdavids/orgeverywhere.git \
    "$HOME/Library/Application Support/Sublime Text/Packages/OrgEverywhere"

# Linux
git clone https://github.com/ihdavids/orgeverywhere.git \
    ~/.config/sublime-text/Packages/OrgEverywhere
    # Windows
git clone https://github.com/ihdavids/orgeverywhere.git "$env:APPDATA\Sublime Text\Packages\OrgEverywhere"

    Then install the libraries: run Package Control: Satisfy Libraries (called Satisfy Dependencies in older Package Control versions) and restart Sublime. Package Control reads the list from the package's dependencies.json: pathlib, pyyaml, dateutil, requests, regex, websocket and six. If OrgEverywhere fails to load with an ImportError for one of them in the console (View > Show Console), that library did not install; run Satisfy Libraries again.

    The connection to the orgs server itself uses only the python standard library (no requests).

    The python 3.8 host

    Sublime Text 4 has two plugin hosts, python 3.3 and python 3.8. A package picks one with a .python-version file at its top level; OrgEverywhere's says 3.8. If you copy the package somewhere by hand, copy that file too: without it Sublime loads OrgEverywhere into the 3.3 host and it fails to start (the console shows import or syntax errors from orgs/).

    Checking that it works

    1. Make a file whose name ends in .org and open it. The syntax in the bottom right corner says OrgEverywhere.
    2. Type a heading (* Hello), put the cursor on it and press tab: the heading folds and unfolds.
    3. The status bar shows the orgs connection (orgs: http://localhost:8010 (you), orgs: offline…). Without a server, run Org: Set Up a Local orgs Server (see A Local orgs Server) or see Connecting to orgs.

    Several other syntaxes come with the package: orgagenda, orgdatepicker, orgdateeditor, orginput and OrgBeancount. They are used by OrgEverywhere's own views; you never need to set a file to them.

    Colour schemes

    OrgEverywhere colours org files with its own scheme, set in its settings (color_scheme). There are two: OrgEverywhere.sublime-color-scheme (dark) and OrgEverywhere-Light.sublime-color-scheme.

    • Org Select Color Scheme picks one of the built in schemes, or one you generated.
    • Org Create Color Scheme From Active, run from a non org file, takes the colour scheme you use for everything else and writes an org flavoured copy of it to Packages/User/OrgColorSchemes/<name>_Org.sublime-color-scheme, with comments on which scopes to tweak. It only works with .sublime-color-scheme files, not older .tmTheme ones, and it switches the agenda and date picker views to the new scheme as well.

    Next

    • Connecting to orgs: start a server and log in.
    • Keys: the default key bindings.
    • Settings: where settings live and how to change them.

    A Local orgs Server

    The quick way

    OrgEverywhere needs an orgs server for everything that looks across your files. If you do not have one, let OrgEverywhere set one up on this machine: run Org: Set Up a Local orgs Server. When Sublime starts and finds no server it offers this once by itself.

    1. It looks up the latest orgs release on github and asks before downloading it.
    2. You pick the folder of org files orgs should read: one of the project's folders, or any other.

    3. You pick how Sublime logs in:

      • Log me in automatically. Sublime makes the user sublimetext with a random password, keeps the password in your OS keychain (without one, in a file only you can read), and logs in with it. You are never asked.
      • Ask me to log in. You choose a user name and password of your own. Sublime asks for them when it needs a login, like any other server's (and with orgsRememberLogin, only once).
    4. It downloads orgs, checks it against the release's checksums.txt, writes its config, starts it, and points orgsUrl at it.

    That is all. The agenda, capture, refile and the rest work from then on.

    What it sets up

    Everything is in one folder of your user data, not in Packages (which people sync, and which would carry the server's keys with it):

    macOS ~/Library/Application Support/OrgEverywhere/orgs
    Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\OrgEverywhere\orgs
    Linux ~/.local/share/OrgEverywhere/orgs
    • orgs (orgs.exe): the server and command line, one binary.
    • orgs.yaml: its config. Yours to edit.
    • keystore.yaml: who may log in.
    • server.crt, server.key: a self-signed certificate (orgs cert).
    • server.log: what the server printed since Sublime last started it.

    The server serves https and nothing else, answers this machine only, and does not run code blocks unless you turn that on in its config. Sublime trusts its certificate, and only for it; you do not need orgsNoVerify or orgsCaFile for it. It runs in the background, outlives Sublime, and every window shares it. When Sublime starts and it is not running, Sublime starts it (orgsServerAutoStart).

    The local server's menu

    Org: Local orgs Server (or Org: orgs, which has the login and connection too) has everything else:

    • Start, Stop, Restart.
    • Check for an update. Sublime also looks once a day by itself (orgsServerCheckForUpdates) and offers a newer release: update, read the release notes, skip that version, or not now.
    • Edit its config. Saving orgs.yaml reloads the server at once; when a change needs a restart (the port, orgDirs, the keystore) Sublime says so and offers it.
    • Show its log.
    • Open worg in the browser, logged in for you.
    • Trust its certificate in browsers, so they stop warning about it.
    • Use it from a terminal. The orgs beside the server reads its orgs.yaml, keys and all, so it needs no login: copy an alias for it.
    • Users and passwords (Org: Manage orgs Users): add a login of your own for worg or the command line, change a password, remove a user.
    • Copy its password: sublimetext's, to log in by hand.

    Users

    sublimetext is Sublime's own login and is left alone. To use worg in a browser or orgs login from somewhere else, add yourself a user with Org: Manage orgs Users:

    • Adding a user goes to the running server (POST /users/add) and works at once. The password does not travel: a salted hash of it does, as with a login.
    • Changing a password or removing a user edits the keystore with the orgs user command line, so the server stops for the moment it takes and starts again.

    To stop logging in automatically, set orgsServerAutoLogin to false and log in as a user of your own (Org: Log out of orgs, then Org: Log in to orgs).

    The same server in VS Code

    The vscode plugin (Org Everywhere for VS Code) sets up a server the same way, with a login of its own (vscode). Each keeps its own copy. To share one, point the other at it: set orgsUrl here (or org.orgsConnection in VS Code) to its address and log in as a user of your own on it.

    Connecting to orgs

    Why a server

    OrgEverywhere edits the org file in front of you by itself. Everything that needs your other files - the agenda, capture, refile, archiving, clocking, day pages, id and custom id links, backlinks, tag completion, query search

    • comes from an orgs server. The server

    keeps your org files parsed and answers for Sublime, VSCode, the orgs command line and the worg web page alike, so they all see the same data.

    The server reads what is saved on disk. A buffer with unsaved changes is not part of the agenda until you save it.

    Running a server

    The quickest way is to let OrgEverywhere do it: Org: Set Up a Local orgs Server downloads orgs, sets it up and runs it (see A Local orgs Server). To run one yourself, install orgs (see its README), then tell it where your org files are in its orgs.yaml:

    server:
  orgDirs:
    - "/Users/me/org"
  keystore: "orgs_keystore.yaml"

    Add a user for yourself and start the server:

    orgs user add me        # asks for a password, twice
orgs serve

    Until a keystore is set the only account is the built in admin with password default; the server warns about that every time it starts. orgs serve listens on http port 8010 and, when https is turned on, on port 443. The orgs documentation covers the rest of its configuration.

    The old OrgEverywhere settings orgDirs, orgFiles, orgExcludeDirs and orgExcludeFiles are no longer read for this: the server's orgDirs decide which files are org files.

    How OrgEverywhere finds the server

    When Sublime starts, OrgEverywhere looks for a server:

    1. If orgsUrl is set, it uses that url and nothing else.
    2. Otherwise it tries each url in orgsDiscoverUrls in order, by default http://localhost:8010 then https://localhost:443, and takes the first that answers like an orgs server.

    A url "answers like an orgs server" when GET /salt returns a json salt (the one orgs route that needs no login). A web server that happens to be on that port is passed over. Each discovery probe waits up to two seconds; a probe of orgsUrl waits orgsTimeout seconds (15).

    If nothing answers, the status bar says orgs: offline and OrgEverywhere looks again every orgsRetrySeconds (60; 0 stops it). Start the server and it connects by itself within a minute, or run Org: Connect to orgs server to connect now.

    To point OrgEverywhere at a server somewhere else run Org: Set orgs server url. It writes orgsUrl into your user settings and connects. Or set it yourself:

    "orgsUrl": "https://myserver.example.com:8443",

    Logging in

    Once a server is found OrgEverywhere checks the login it stored last time for that url. If the server still accepts it you are connected without being asked.

    Otherwise it asks, in the input panel at the bottom of the window:

    1. orgs user for <url>: - prefilled with the last user name you logged in with on that server, or orgsUser.
    2. orgs password for <user>@<url>: - what you type shows as dots.

    The password itself never leaves Sublime. OrgEverywhere asks the server for your salt, sends a salted sha256 hash of the password in its place, and forgets what you typed. The server answers with a session token.

    With orgsPromptLoginOnStartup (on by default) the prompt appears as soon as Sublime starts. Turn it off and you are asked the first time a feature needs the server instead. Org: Log in to orgs logs in at any time, for example as a different user.

    A server running with noAuth needs no login; the status bar shows (no auth) in place of a user name.

    What is kept, and where

    OrgEverywhere keeps your login per server url so a restart does not ask again. It keeps it in the operating system's secret store when there is one:

    System Store Found under
    macOS Keychain (/usr/bin/security) service OrgEverywhere.orgs, account orgs:<url>
    Windows Credential Manager generic credential OrgEverywhere.orgs:orgs:<url>
    Linux Secret Service (secret-tool) service OrgEverywhere.orgs, account orgs:<url>

    What is stored:

    • Always: your user name, the session token and when it expires.
    • With orgsRememberLogin (on by default): the salted password hash as well, so that when the session expires OrgEverywhere logs back in by itself instead of asking. Anyone who can read your keychain entry can log in to that server as you with it, so turn the setting off if that matters to you.
    • Never: the password you typed.

    Without a secret store (a Linux machine with no keyring running, for instance) the login goes to a file instead, <Sublime cache>/OrgEverywhere/orgs_logins.json, readable only by you (mode 0600, in a 0700 directory). The file holds the token only, never the password hash, so once the session expires you are asked again. orgsCredentialStore: "file" uses the file even when a secret store exists.

    Org: Log out of orgs (forget stored login) ends the session and deletes everything stored for that server.

    Staying logged in

    A session token has an expiry date. OrgEverywhere renews it with the server when three quarters of its lifetime has passed, and again whenever a request is made in its last two minutes, so a Sublime that is in use stays logged in.

    When the token has expired anyway (Sublime was closed for a week, the server was restarted with new keys) the next request is refused. Then:

    1. With a remembered login, OrgEverywhere logs in again silently and retries. If the server refuses the stored hash (the password was changed) the hash is dropped.
    2. Otherwise the login prompt appears and the command that hit the refusal fails with orgs: log in, then try again. Log in and run the command again: nothing waits on the prompt, so Sublime never hangs on a login. If you cancel the prompt it does not reappear for 15 seconds.

    https and self signed certificates

    A server with a certificate from a public authority needs nothing extra. A self signed certificate is not trusted by default, and discovery reports certificate not trusted (self signed? ...). Either trust that certificate:

    "orgsCaFile": "~/dev/orgs/server.crt",

    or turn verification off, which lets anything on the network pretend to be your server:

    "orgsNoVerify": true,

    A server on another machine

    The server reports file names as they are on its own disk. When it runs on another machine, or in a container, those paths mean nothing here. Map the server's path prefixes to where the same files are on this machine (synced with Dropbox, git, syncthing…):

    "orgsPathMap": {
    "/home/me/org": "~/Dropbox/org",
    "/data/work":   "D:\\work\\org"
},

    Keys are server paths, values local paths; ~ is expanded. The longest matching prefix wins, and the map is used both ways: server paths are turned into local ones to open files, and local paths into server ones when OrgEverywhere asks about the file you are editing. A server on this machine needs no map.

    Saving before the server writes

    Refile, archive, agenda actions and the server's capture templates are carried out by the server, which writes the file on disk. If that file is open in Sublime with unsaved changes, the next save would quietly undo what the server wrote. So with orgsSaveBeforeServerEdits (on by default) OrgEverywhere saves the buffer first and waits for the server to re-read it. Turn it off and those commands refuse with "save it first" instead.

    The server also tells OrgEverywhere when files change underneath it (an event stream, orgsEvents), which keeps ids, backlinks and the agenda current when you edit files outside Sublime.

    The status bar

    Org files show the connection in the status bar (orgsShowStatus):

    Status bar Meaning
    orgs: <url> (<user>) connected and logged in
    orgs: <url> (no auth) connected to a server that needs no login
    orgs: login needed (<url>) the server is there, you are not logged in
    orgs: connecting... looking for the server
    orgs: offline no server found; looking again every minute
    (nothing) orgsEnabled is false

    Commands

    Command What it does
    Org: Connect to orgs server find the server now and log in; says why when none is found
    Org: Log in to orgs show the login prompt
    Org: Log out of orgs (forget stored login) end the session and delete the stored login
    Org: Set orgs server url set orgsUrl and connect
    Org: orgs connection status what the connection is doing, and why
    Org: orgs reload server config have the server re-read its yaml (capture templates, filters…)

    Troubleshooting

    Start with Org: orgs connection status. It shows:

    • State: connected, login, searching, unavailable or disabled.
    • Detail: why, when there is a reason - each url tried and what it answered, session expired, logged out.
    • Server, User and Session expires.
    • Login stored in: which store is used (macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager, Secret Service, or the file), and Remembered login: whether a password hash is kept so expired sessions log back in by themselves.
    • Live updates: whether the server's change events are coming in.
    • Files tracked: how many org files the server knows about.
    • With no server at all, Looking at: the urls being tried.
    Symptom Try
    Could not find an orgs server is orgs serve running, on the port in orgsUrl / orgsDiscoverUrls?
    connection refused for every url the server is not running, or listens on another port
    answered, but is not an orgs server something else owns that port; set orgsUrl
    certificate not trusted set orgsCaFile (or orgsNoVerify)
    orgs: login needed Org: Log in to orgs
    login failed: wrong user name or password check the user with orgs user ls on the server's machine
    asked to log in after every restart no secret store, so only the token is kept; see above
    headings open the wrong file or none a remote server needs orgsPathMap
    a change is missing from the agenda save the file: the server reads what is on disk
    Files tracked: 0 the server's orgDirs are wrong or empty

    For more detail set "enableDebugLogging": true (or the environment variable SUBLIME_ORGEVERYWHERE_DEBUG) and watch the console (View > Show Console): connection messages start with orgs:.

    Working without a server

    Set orgsEnabled to false, or just do not run one. Editing works as always: folding, todo states, tables, source blocks, links within the file, exporting the file. The features that need your other files say orgs: not connected instead of showing nothing.

    Keys

    Where the keys come from

    Sublime loads a package's key bindings from Default.sublime-keymap and Default (Windows|OSX|Linux).sublime-keymap. OrgEverywhere has only the first, so its keys are the same on every platform: alt+o is alt+o on macOS too (option+o), not cmd+o. These are the default keys listed below. (The package also contains an OrgEverywhere.sublime-keymap; Sublime does not load a file by that name, so its bindings do nothing.)

    Most keys are a chord: alt+o followed by one or more letters. alt+o i h means press alt+o, let go, press i, then h. They only work in an org file (or the view named in the heading of the table); the few global keys are opt-in, see Global keys (opt-in) below.

    To change a key, open Preferences > Package Settings > Org Everywhere > Key Bindings: OrgEverywhere's bindings are on the left, yours on the right. Copy a line across and change its keys. Every command, bound or not, is also in the command palette under its caption (Org …).

    Global keys (opt-in)

    Every default key works only in an org file (or the view named in its table below). A few commands are useful from anywhere: capturing a note, opening the agenda, making a link to the line you are on. Keys for those would be live in every view, taking keys that other packages or you may want, so they are not on by default. They are in an example keymap instead, Example Global.sublime-keymap, which Sublime does not load.

    To turn them on, open Preferences > Package Settings > Org Everywhere > Example Global Key Bindings: the examples are on the left, your own keymap on the right. Copy the bindings you want across, and change their keys if you like.

    [
    { "keys": ["ctrl+shift+x"],    "command": "org_capture"            },
    { "keys": ["alt+o", "z"],      "command": "org_capture"            },
    { "keys": ["ctrl+alt+x"],      "command": "org_open_refile"        },
    { "keys": ["alt+o", "a", "d"], "command": "org_agenda_day_view"    },
    { "keys": ["alt+o", "o", "a"], "command": "org_agenda_custom_view" },
    { "keys": ["alt+o", "y", "l"], "command": "org_create_link"        },
    { "keys": ["alt+o", "d", "c"], "command": "org_day_page_create"    },
]

    alt+o o a org_agenda_custom_view Org Agenda Custom View

    The views orgs commands open (habits, clock report, full text search results, file history…):

    Keys Command What it does
    enter org_orgs_goto_row open the heading or line
    g org_orgs_refresh_view ask the server again
    t org_orgs_habit_toggle mark the habit done today

    In the tag and id inputs that offer completions, up and down move through the suggestions.

    With NeoVintageous

    If you use NeoVintageous, a second set of bindings works in command (normal) mode with space as the leader in place of alt+o: space i h inserts a sibling heading, space c i clocks in, and so on for every alt+o key above, plus:

    Keys Command
    Z org_capture
    shift+space org_agenda_day_view
    R org_refile
    space i m org_insert_tag
    space r m org_remove_tag
    space r a m org_remove_all_tags
    space r f org_refile_to_file
    space r r org_refile_to_file_and_headline
    space f o org_fold_all_but_me (fold the rest)
    space f m org_fix_tags
    space f s save
    space 1 … space 5 focus editor group 1 to 5
    space t e org_edit_formula_for_cell (table)
    space t k org_clear_cell (table)

    In the agenda in command mode t changes the todo state (s without NeoVintageous), and f f reopens the filter view.

    Unbound commands

    Many commands have no key: the folding commands (Org Fold All, Org Unfold All…), Org Jump In File, Org Insert Property, Org Sort List, Org Insert Tag and most of the orgs commands. Run them from the command palette, or give them keys of your own:

    // Packages/User/Default (OSX).sublime-keymap (or Windows / Linux)
[
    { "keys": ["alt+o", "j"], "command": "org_jump_in_file",
      "context": [{ "key": "selector", "operand": "text.orgmode" }] },
    { "keys": ["alt+o", "i", "g"], "command": "org_insert_tag",
      "context": [{ "key": "selector", "operand": "text.orgmode" }] },
]

    Settings

    Where settings live

    OrgEverywhere's settings are in OrgEverywhere.sublime-settings. Sublime merges two copies of that file:

    1. Packages/OrgEverywhere/OrgEverywhere.sublime-settings: the defaults that come with the package, with a comment on every setting. Do not edit it; an upgrade replaces it.
    2. Packages/User/OrgEverywhere.sublime-settings: yours. A setting here wins over the default.

    Preferences > Package Settings > Org Everywhere > Settings opens both side by side, the defaults on the left and yours on the right.

    On its first start OrgEverywhere copies the whole default file into Packages/User if you have none. That copy then pins every setting at the value it had in that version, including settings a later version changes. It is a good idea to trim your file down to the settings you actually changed:

    // Packages/User/OrgEverywhere.sublime-settings
{
    "orgsUrl": "https://myserver:8443",
    "orgsCaFile": "~/orgs/server.crt",
    "tagColumn": 70,
    "startup": ["content"],
}

    Because the org syntax is called OrgEverywhere, this file is also the syntax specific settings file for org views: ordinary Sublime settings in it (color_scheme, auto_complete, word_wrap, tab_size…) apply to org files only. The agenda and the date picker have their own (orgagenda.sublime-settings, orgdatepicker.sublime-settings), which is where their colour schemes are set.

    When a change takes effect

    Most settings are read each time they are used, so a change applies to the next command. The connection settings (orgsUrl, orgsCaFile, orgsNoVerify, orgsPathMap, orgsCredentialStore…) are read when OrgEverywhere connects: run Org: Connect to orgs server after changing them. Settings that are read when a file is opened (startup) apply to files opened afterwards.

    Values that refer to other values

    A string setting can use {date}, {time} and {datetime} (now), and the name of any other setting in braces, which is replaced by that setting's value. The default capture templates do this: their target is ["file", "{refile}"], the refile setting.

    In buffer settings

    Many things can be set for one file instead of globally, with a keyword line near the top of the file, as in Emacs org mode:

    #+STARTUP: content logdone
#+TODO: TODO NEXT WAITING | DONE CANCELLED
#+PRIORITIES: A B C

    The file's line wins over the global setting (startup, todoStates, priorities…). The guides for each feature say which they read.

    Settings that are no longer used

    Since 2.0 the orgs server decides which files are org files, so orgFiles, orgExcludeDirs and orgExcludeFiles are ignored, and orgDirs is only used to look for images when exporting without a server. Set orgDirs in the server's orgs.yaml instead. See Connecting to orgs.

    Reference

    Every setting, with its default and what it does, is listed under Reference > Settings. The orgs connection settings are explained in Connecting to orgs.

    To see what OrgEverywhere is doing, set "enableDebugLogging": true and open the console (View > Show Console).

    Editing

    Working in an org file: headings, folding, moving around, lists, properties, priorities and dates. All of this works on the buffer as you type, with or without a server.

    Headings and Text

    The outline

    An org file is an outline. A line starting with stars is a heading, and the number of stars is its level. Everything up to the next heading of the same or a higher level belongs to it: its text, and its children.

    * Project                                                     :work:
  Some notes about the project.
** TODO [#A] Write the proposal
   SCHEDULED: <2026-10-12 Mon>
** Meeting notes
* Home

    A heading line can carry a todo state (TODO), a priority ([#A], see Priorities) and tags (:work:) as well as its title. Below it come planning lines (SCHEDULED:, DEADLINE:, see Dates and Times), drawers (see Properties and Drawers) and then any text.

    Two words this manual uses:

    • A subtree is a heading with everything under it, children included.
    • An entity is a heading with only its own text, up to its first child.

    Text formatting

    You write You get
    *bold* bold
    /italic/ italic
    _underline_ underline
    +strikethrough+ strikethrough
    ~code~ code
    =verbatim= verbatim

    Sublime highlights them as you type; they matter most when you export (see Exporting).

    Adding headings

    • Org Insert Heading Sibling (alt+o i h) adds a heading at the same level after the current subtree and puts the cursor on its title.
    • Org Insert Heading Child (alt+o i c) adds a heading one level deeper at the end of the current subtree, after any children it already has.

    ctrl+enter does what you most likely mean at the cursor: a new list item in a list, a new checkbox after a checkbox, the next number in a numbered list, and a sibling heading anywhere else in a heading. ctrl+shift+enter is its twin: the new item goes at the end of the list, and on a heading it adds a child instead of a sibling.

    enter on a heading line starts a new line indented to the heading's text, so the body lines up under the title.

    The heading snippets do the same from the keyboard: type h, hh, hhh, hhhh or hhhhh and press tab for a heading of that level.

    Changing a heading's level

    • Org Change Indent (alt+o right) demotes the heading: one more star, and its text and all its children move with it.
    • Org Change DeIndent (alt+o left) promotes it.

    On a list item the same keys indent or outdent the item and its sub items (see Lists and Checkboxes).

    Moving headings

    Org Move Heading Up (alt+o up) and Org Move Heading Down (alt+o down) swap the subtree at the cursor with its previous or next sibling. A heading only moves among its siblings: it does not leave its parent. To move a subtree somewhere else, in this file or another, refile it (alt+o R, see Planning).

    Selecting and copying

    Keys Command Selects or copies
    alt+o m s Org Select Subtree the heading and everything under it
    alt+o m e Org Select Entity the heading and its text, without children
    alt+o y s Org Copy Subtree the subtree, to the clipboard
    alt+o y e Org Copy Entity the entity, to the clipboard

    With NeoVintageous the copies also go into its unnamed register, so p pastes them.

    Tags

    Tags sit at the end of a heading line between colons, :work:urgent:. A heading also has the tags of the headings above it, and of the file's #+FILETAGS: line, for searching and the agenda.

    • Org Insert Tag asks for a tag and adds it to the heading at the cursor. The input offers the tags already in use: with an orgs server, every tag in every org file; without one, the tags of the files you have open. You can also type a new tag. Adding a tag the heading already has does nothing.
    • Org Remove Tag asks for a tag and removes it.
    • Org Remove All Tags removes them all.
    • Org Insert Archive Tag adds the ARCHIVE tag.
    • Org Fix Tags lines up the tags of every heading in the file.

    The tags are aligned so they start at column tagColumn (default 80, kept between 30 and 150). A heading longer than that gets its tags right after the title.

    The tag input has no default key (alt+o i t is the timestamp); with NeoVintageous it is space i m. See Keys to bind one.

    Todo states

    alt+o t on a heading opens a list of todo states to pick from (on a checkbox it toggles the checkbox instead). Todo states, logging when a task is done and repeating tasks are covered under Planning.

    Snippets

    Type the trigger and press tab:

    Trigger Inserts
    <s a source block, cursor on the language
    <e an example block
    <q a quote block
    <v a verse block
    <n a notes block
    <b a dynamic block (#+BEGIN: / #+END:)
    <l a link *description*
    h … hhhhh a heading of level 1 to 5
    t a tag :TAG:
    p a page separator --- YYYY-MM-DD ---

    Your own snippets work too: any .sublime-snippet with the scope text.orgmode in your Packages/User folder.

    Folding

    Tab

    tab is the key that makes an org file feel like org. What it does depends on where the cursor is:

    Cursor on tab
    a heading line cycles the heading: folded, children, whole subtree
    a property drawer or other drawer folds or unfolds the drawer
    a dynamic block (#+BEGIN:) folds or unfolds the block
    a link shows or hides the link's target
    a checkbox with sub items folds or unfolds the sub items
    text before the first heading cycles the whole file: overview, contents, show all
    a table moves to the next cell
    anywhere else the usual: completes, expands a snippet, or a tab

    Cycling a heading

    tab on a heading moves it through three states:

    1. Folded: only the heading line shows.
    2. Children: the heading's text and its child headings show, each child folded.
    3. Subtree: everything under it shows.

    Then back to folded.

    Cycling the whole file

    shift+tab on any heading (or tab above the first heading) cycles the whole file:

    1. Overview: top level headings only.
    2. Contents: every heading, no text - a table of contents.
    3. Show all: everything, with drawers folded.

    Emacs can narrow the buffer to one subtree. Sublime cannot, so the nearest thing is to fold everything else: Org Fold Others (space f o with NeoVintageous) folds every heading that is not the current one or above it.

    Folding commands

    None of these has a default key; run them from the command palette or bind them (see Keys).

    Command Does
    Org Fold All fold every heading
    Org Unfold All unfold every heading
    Org Fold Contents every heading visible, their text folded (contents view)
    Org Fold Others fold everything except the current heading and its parents
    Org Fold All Links hide the targets of all links, showing only descriptions
    Org Fold Thing fold the current selection
    Org Remove All Folds unfold everything in the file, drawers and links too

    How a file opens

    When an org file is opened its folds are set from its #+STARTUP: line, or the startup setting when it has none (default ["showall"]):

    Startup word The file opens
    overview or fold top level headings only
    content all headings, no text
    showall (default) everything, drawers folded 
    #+STARTUP: overview

    Links are always shown folded (description only) when a file opens.

    With onFocusRespectStartupFolds set to true, switching back to an overview or content file folds everything but the heading you are in.

    When folds go wrong

    OrgEverywhere's folds are Sublime folds placed by position. After big edits outside OrgEverywhere (a file changed on disk, a large paste) a fold can end up in the wrong place. Save the file and run Org Remove All Folds; then fold again.

    Folding is per view: the same file in two tabs can be folded differently.

    Moving Around

    Heading to heading

    • Org Up (ctrl+up) jumps to the heading above the cursor.
    • Org Down (ctrl+down) jumps to the heading below it.

    They stop at the next heading line, whatever its level.

    Jumping within the file

    Org Jump In File lists every heading of the current file, indented by level, in a quick panel. Type a few letters of a heading and press enter to go there.

    It has no default key; it is worth binding one (see Keys).

    Sublime's own Goto Symbol (ctrl+r, cmd+r on macOS) also lists the headings of an org file.

    Jumping to a custom id

    A CUSTOM_ID property names a heading, like a bookmark:

    * John Smith
  :PROPERTIES:
  :CUSTOM_ID: johnsmith
  :END:

    Org Jump To CustomId lists every custom id in every org file the orgs server knows, with its heading and file, and opens the one you pick. Because the list comes from the server it needs a connection; if the file is open and you have moved the heading since saving, OrgEverywhere finds it in the buffer rather than at the line the server last saw.

    Custom ids should be unique across your files. Org Insert CustomId (alt+o i i) adds one to the heading at the cursor, offering the ids already in use so you can see which are taken; spaces become -.

    A link [[#johnsmith]] jumps to that heading too, and id: links find headings by their ID property; links are covered under Links.

    Other places to jump to

    These are covered with the features they belong to:

    • Org Jump To Clock: the heading the clock is running on (see Planning).
    • Org Jump To Today and Org: Jump To Marker: the heading carrying the today marker or another orgs marker (see Planning).
    • Org Jump To Backlink: a heading that links to this one (see Links).
    • Org: orgs Query Search and Org: orgs Full Text Search: any heading or line in any file (see orgs Server).
    • In the agenda, enter opens the heading of the line under the cursor.

    Lists and Checkboxes

    Kinds of list

    - a plain list item
- another
  - a sub item, indented under its parent

+ plus works the same as minus

1. numbered items
2. end in a dot
3) or a parenthesis

- term :: a description list item

    Items nest by indentation: an item belongs to the nearest less indented item above it. Numbered lists use digits only; Emacs' lettered lists (a., b.) are not recognised.

    Adding items

    On a list item:

    • ctrl+enter adds an item after this one (after its sub items, if it has any), with the same bullet and indentation. On a checkbox item the new item gets an empty checkbox; in a numbered list it gets the next number and the items after it are renumbered.
    • ctrl+shift+enter adds the item at the end of the list instead.

    On a heading the same keys add a sibling or child heading (see Headings and Text).

    Indenting items

    Org Change Indent (alt+o right) indents the item at the cursor by two spaces, and Org Change DeIndent (alt+o left) outdents it. Its sub items move with it.

    Numbered lists

    Keeping numbers in order by hand is tedious, so:

    • Org Update Numbered List renumbers the list at the cursor: 1, 2, 3… at each level of indentation, keeping each item's . or ).
    • Org Append Numbered List adds the next item after the cursor, like ctrl+enter.
    • alt+o c c (Org Recalc, which recalculates whatever is at the cursor) renumbers the list too.

    Checkboxes

    A list item that starts with [ ] is a checkbox, a small todo:

    * Packing [1/3]
  - [X] passport
  - [-] clothes [1/2]
    - [X] shirts
    - [ ] socks
  - [ ] tickets
    Box Means
    [ ] not done
    [X] done ([x] works too)
    [-] some of its sub items are done

    • alt+o t (or Org Checkbox Toggle) toggles the checkbox at the cursor. Its sub items follow it, and the boxes and summaries of the items and heading above it are updated: a parent whose children are all done is checked, one with some done gets [-].
    • tab on a checkbox that has sub items folds them away.
    Summaries

    A [/] or [%] cookie on a parent item or a heading shows how many of the checkboxes below it are done: [2/5] or [40%].

    • Org Add Checkbox Summary (alt+o c s) adds a [/] cookie to the line at the cursor and fills it in.
    • Toggling a checkbox updates the cookies above it.
    • Org Recalc Checkbox recalculates the cookie at the cursor; Org Recalc All Checkbox recalculates every cookie in the file, as does alt+o c c outside a table or block.

    A cookie counts the checkboxes directly under it. To count the sub items of sub items too, set checkboxSummaryRecursive to true, or for one heading set its COOKIE_DATA property to recursive (or notrecursive to override the setting):

    * Packing [3/5]
  :PROPERTIES:
  :COOKIE_DATA: recursive
  :END:

    Sorting a list

    Org Sort List sorts the list the cursor is in alphabetically by the text of its items (after the bullet, number or checkbox). Each item keeps its sub items. A numbered list is renumbered afterwards.

    - pears                - apples
- apples         =>    - oranges
- oranges              - pears

    It sorts -, + and numbered lists, A to Z only, and compares characters as they are, so capitals come before lower case letters. It has no default key.

    Properties and Drawers

    Drawers

    A drawer is a named block of lines under a heading, between :NAME: and :END:. It holds things you want with the heading but out of sight: metadata, logs, notes to yourself. Drawers are not exported.

    * Chapter 3
  :NOTES:
  Remember to foreshadow the storm.
  :END:
  The chapter's text...

    Drawers are folded when a file opens; tab on a drawer line opens and closes it (see Folding).

    Org Insert Drawer asks for a name and adds an empty drawer to the heading at the cursor, after its planning lines and property drawer. A heading only gets one drawer of each name: if it already has one, nothing happens.

    Properties

    The PROPERTIES drawer holds key value pairs. It comes right after the heading (and its SCHEDULED: / DEADLINE: lines):

    * Kind of Blue
  :PROPERTIES:
  :ARTIST:   Miles Davis
  :YEAR:     1959
  :CUSTOM_ID: kindofblue
  :END:

    Properties turn headings into records: the column view, tables, the agenda and the orgs query language can all read them. Some names mean something to org itself: ID and CUSTOM_ID identify a heading, Effort is an estimate, COOKIE_DATA changes checkbox counting, LAST_REPEAT is written when a repeating task is done.

    • Org Insert Property Drawer adds an empty PROPERTIES drawer.
    • Org Insert Property asks for a name and then a value, and sets that property on the heading at the cursor. A property that is already there gets the new value; otherwise it is added, along with the drawer if there is none. Names are matched without regard to case.

    Properties with their own commands
    Command Sets
    Org Insert CustomId (alt+o i i) CUSTOM_ID, from a name you type (spaces become -); offers the ids already in use
    Org Create Heading Id ID, a new uuid, unless the heading already has one
    Org Insert Effort Effort, an estimate such as 2h, 1d 4h or 30min; a bare number gets the unit in defaultEffortEstimateUnit (d)
    Org Insert Created Property Created, now as an inactive timestamp

    ID and CUSTOM_ID are what id: and #custom-id links point at, and what the orgs server uses to find a heading again after it has moved. See Links and Moving Around.

    The logbook

    The LOGBOOK drawer is where org writes history: clock lines when you clock in and out, and state changes, for example when a repeating task is marked done:

    ** TODO Water the plants
   SCHEDULED: <2026-10-14 Wed +1w>
   :PROPERTIES:
   :LAST_REPEAT: [2026-10-07 Wed 09:12]
   :END:
   :LOGBOOK:
   - State "DONE"       from "TODO"       [2026-10-07 Wed 09:12]
   CLOCK: [2026-10-07 Wed 08:40]--[2026-10-07 Wed 09:10] =>  0:30
   :END:

    You rarely write it yourself. Clocking and repeating tasks are covered under Planning; see also Dates and Times.

    In buffer settings

    Lines starting with #+ set things for the whole file, the way properties do for a heading:

    #+TITLE: My Novel
#+STARTUP: overview
#+PRIORITIES: A B C
#+FILETAGS: :writing:

    Exporting reads many more (#+OPTIONS:, #+ATTR_HTML:, #+LATEX_HEADER:…), see Exporting. The org manual's In-buffer settings lists them all; OrgEverywhere supports a subset.

    Further reading

    • Drawers in the org manual
    • Property syntax

    Priorities

    Priority cookies

    A priority is a cookie after the todo state on a heading line:

    * Projects
** TODO [#A] Renew the passport
** TODO [#B] Book the flights
** TODO Pack

    A priority means nothing to org beyond what you make of it: the agenda can sort and filter by it, queries can ask for it. A heading without one has none.

    Changing a priority

    Org Change Priority (alt+o p) lists the priorities; pick one to set it on the heading at the cursor, replacing any it had. Pick none to remove it.

    In the agenda , changes the priority of the heading on that line.

    Which priorities there are

    By default A to E. Change the list for all files with the priorities setting:

    "priorities": ["A", "B", "C"],

    or for one file with a #+PRIORITIES: line, which wins over the setting:

    #+PRIORITIES: 1 2 3 4 5

    Unlike Emacs, where #+PRIORITIES: gives the highest, lowest and default priority, OrgEverywhere takes the line as the full list to choose from, in order.

    Priorities can be letters or digits. A to E each have their own colour in the OrgEverywhere colour schemes; any other priority is coloured as a general priority.

    Dates and Times

    Timestamps

    A timestamp is a date, optionally with a time:

    Written Is
    <2026-10-12 Mon> active: it puts the heading on the agenda that day
    <2026-10-12 Mon 14:00> active, with a time
    <2026-10-12 Mon 14:00-15:30> a time range on one day
    <2026-10-12 Mon>--<2026-10-14 Wed> a range of days
    [2026-10-12 Mon] inactive: a note of when, never on the agenda
    <2026-10-12 Mon +1w> repeating: every week from that date

    The weekday is for you to read; the date is what counts.

    Scheduled, deadline, or an appointment

    Which kind of date to use depends on what the heading is:

    • SCHEDULED - when you plan to start working on it. The task shows on the agenda from that day on, every day, until you mark it done.
    • DEADLINE - when it has to be done by. The agenda warns you about it ahead of time (14 days by default, or what the timestamp says: <2026-10-30 Fri -3d> warns three days ahead), and it stays on the agenda, overdue, until it is done.
    • A plain active timestamp - an appointment: a meeting, a doctor's visit. It shows on that day only (every occurrence, if it repeats).
    ** TODO Write the report
   DEADLINE: <2026-10-30 Fri -3d>
** TODO Start the garden plan
   SCHEDULED: <2026-10-12 Mon>
** Lunch with Sam
   <2026-10-15 Thu 12:30>

    The agenda is worked out by the orgs server, which reads saved files; see Planning for what lands on which day.

    Adding dates

    Keys Command Adds
    alt+o i s Org Schedule a SCHEDULED: line under the heading, date from the picker
    alt+o i e Org Deadline a DEADLINE: line, date from the picker
    alt+o i t Org Timestamp an active timestamp line under the heading
    alt+o i d a Org Insert Date Active an active timestamp at the cursor, from the picker
    alt+o i d i Org Insert Date Inactive an inactive timestamp at the cursor, from the picker
    Org Insert Today Active <today> at the cursor
    Org Insert Today Inactive [today] at the cursor
    Org Insert Now Active <today hh:mm> at the cursor
    Org Insert Now Inactive [today hh:mm] at the cursor
    Org Closed a CLOSED: [now] line under the heading

    Org Schedule, Org Deadline and Org Timestamp always add a new line right under the heading line; they do not replace a SCHEDULED: or DEADLINE: the heading already has, so delete the old one yourself. Cancelling the picker removes the line again.

    Dates picked with the picker always carry a time (the time shown in the picker, which starts at now). Delete the time if you only want the day.

    The date picker

    The date picker opens a view with three months - last month, this month and next - and a clock, and an input line at the bottom of the window holding the date. Change the date in the input line or with the keys, watch the calendar follow, and press enter to use it or escape to cancel.

    Typing a date

    The input line understands:

    Type Means
    . or +0 now
    15 the 15th: this month if that is still ahead, else next month
    3d, 2h, 1d 4h, 30min, 1y now plus that long
    1:30 now plus an hour and a half
    fri, tuesday the next Friday, Tuesday… (a week ahead if it is today)
    mar, mar 15, 15 mar that month (and day) this year
    2026-11-03 Tue 09:00 that date and time, as written in a timestamp

    Offsets are always forward from now: there are no negative offsets, and no w (weeks) unit - use 7d. A leading + is not understood (3d, not +3d).

    Moving with the keys
    Keys Moves the date by
    < / > a day
    ctrl+, / ctrl+. a week
    alt+, / alt+. a month
    ctrl+shift+, / ctrl+shift+. an hour
    alt+shift+, / alt+shift+. a minute
    Picking with the mouse

    alt+click on a day in the calendar picks it. Sublime cannot give a package mouse bindings that only apply in one view, so this needs a mouse map in your User folder: run Preferences > Package Settings > Org Everywhere > Setup MouseMap once. It writes Packages/User/Default.sublime-mousemap (only if you have none; otherwise add its alt+button1 binding to yours by hand, see Open MouseMap in the same menu).

    The first day of the week

    The calendar starts its weeks on firstDayOfWeek (Sunday). Set it to Monday for weeks that start on Monday.

    Repeating dates

    A repeater after the date makes it come round again:

    Repeater Marking the task done moves the date
    +1w one week on from the date it had (it may still be in the past)
    ++1w on by weeks until it is in the future
    .+1w one week on from today

    Units are d, w, m and y. A repeating task does not stay done: changing it to a done state leaves it in its todo state, moves its dates on, and writes LAST_REPEAT and a State "DONE" from "TODO" line in its LOGBOOK. See Planning for todo states and the agenda, and Repeated tasks in the org manual.

    Further reading

    • Dates and times in the org manual

    Planning

    Todo states, the agenda, capture, refile and archive, clocking, day pages and a way of putting them together. These work across all of your org files, through the orgs server.

    Todo States and Workflows

    Todos

    A todo is a heading whose first word is a todo keyword:

    * TODO Write the release notes
* NEXT Call the plumber
* DONE Book the flights

    Todos can sit anywhere: in the middle of meeting notes, in a project file, in your inbox. You do not have to collect them into one list by hand. The agenda and the todo views find them in all of your org files (through the orgs server, see The Agenda), so jot an action down where it comes up and let the agenda gather it.

    Keywords and workflows

    The keywords form a workflow. The words before the vertical bar are active (still to do); the words after it are done:

      "todoStates": ["TODO","NEXT", "BLOCKED","WAITING","FLAG", "CLEANUP", "IN-PROGRESS", "DOING","|", "CANCELLED","REASSIGNED", "DONE","MEETING","PHONE","NOTE", "FIXED"],

    That is the todoStates setting, used for every file without a workflow of its own. A file can have its own with a #+TODO: line at the top:

    #+TODO: REPORT BUG KNOWNCAUSE | FIXED

    The keyword picker offers that file's keywords and the agenda judges that file's headings by them.

    The server's keywords

    The agenda, the todo views, query search and everything else that looks across files come from the orgs server, and the server decides what is active and what is done by the file's own #+TODO: line, or when there is none by its defaultTodoStates setting in orgs.yaml:

    server:
  defaultTodoStates: "TODO INPROGRESS IN-PROGRESS NEXT BLOCKED PAUSED WAITING PHONE MEETING BACKLOG | DONE CANCELLED"

    That is the server's default, and it is not the same list as OrgEverywhere's todoStates: OrgEverywhere counts MEETING and PHONE as done, the server counts them as active, and the server does not know NOTE at all. When the two lists disagree the buffer and the agenda disagree. Either give both the same list, or put a #+TODO: line in your files (both sides read it).

    Changing the state

    • Org Change Todo (org_todo_change) shows the file's keywords and "none" in a quick panel.
    • alt+o t (NeoVintageous: space t) is the toggle: on a checkbox it ticks the box, anywhere else it opens the keyword picker.
    • In the agenda the state is changed on the server (see The Agenda).

    Logging when a task is done

    With #+STARTUP: logdone in the file, moving a heading to a done keyword adds a CLOSED: line with the time; moving it back out of done removes it. #+STARTUP: lognotedone asks for a closing note as well and writes it to the heading's :LOGBOOK:. The logDone setting (true) turns on CLOSED: lines for every file.

    Repeating tasks

    A task whose SCHEDULED, DEADLINE or plain timestamp has a repeater does not stay done. Marking it done keeps its keyword, writes - State "DONE" from "TODO" [time] to its logbook, sets its LAST_REPEAT property and moves the date on:

    • +1w moves it one interval from the old date,
    • ++1w moves it by whole intervals until it is in the future,
    • .+1w moves it one interval from today.
    * TODO Water the plants
  SCHEDULED: <2026-10-12 Mon .+3d>

    A repeating task with :STYLE: habit is a habit: see the habits view in What the Server Adds.

    Scheduled and deadline

    Dates are what put a todo on the agenda:

    • SCHEDULED: is when you plan to start. It is on the agenda that day and, until it is done, it is carried to today as an overdue item.
    • DEADLINE: is when it must be finished. It shows on today for a warning period before (14 days unless the stamp says -3d) and as overdue after.
    • A plain active timestamp <2026-10-12 Mon 10:00> is an appointment: on its day only.

    Org Schedule (alt+o i s) and Org Deadline (alt+o i e) add them with the date picker. The rules for what lands on which day are in The Agenda.

    Priorities

    A priority cookie ([#A]) after the keyword says how much a todo matters; Org Change Priority (alt+o p) sets it. Writing and configuring them is covered in Priorities. For planning they order and narrow things:

    ** TODO [#A] Fix the build
** TODO [#C] Tidy the wiki
    • The agenda's day view sorts entries of the same kind by priority (no priority counts as B); the todo lists sort by date, then priority.
    • A view can keep only some priorities: Todos : priorityfilter |A |B (see The Agenda), and a query can ask IsPriority("A").
    • In the agenda , changes an entry's priority. It offers the priorities setting, not a file's #+PRIORITIES:.

    Tags

    Tags at the end of a heading give it context, and are inherited by everything below it; #+FILETAGS: tags a whole file:

    #+FILETAGS: :work:
* TODO Review the budget                                     :finance:

    The agenda filters by tags (tagfilter) and so does the query language (HasTags("finance")). A heading tagged ARCHIVE is archived: the agenda leaves it and everything under it out.

    The Agenda

    What the agenda is

    The agenda gathers your todos and dated headings from every org file into views: a calendar, a week, today hour by hour, lists of projects, next actions and loose tasks. You act on the entries from there: change their state, clock in, jump to them.

    Since 2.0 the agenda comes from the orgs server. The server works out what lands on each day (GET /agenda) and which headings a list shows (GET /agenda/nodes); OrgEverywhere draws it. The agenda in Sublime, worg, VSCode and orgs agenda on the command line therefore agree. Without a connected server the agenda says so instead of showing an empty day.

    Saved files only

    The server reads files from disk. A buffer with unsaved changes is not in the agenda until you save it; the agenda says how many are waiting ("2 unsaved org buffers are not in the agenda - save to include them"). Set agendaSaveBeforeRender to true to have them saved before the agenda is fetched.

    Opening the agenda

    Command Keys What it does
    Org Agenda Custom View alt+o o a (global, opt-in; NeoVintageous space o a) the Default view of AgendaCustomViews
    Org Agenda Choose View pick one of your AgendaCustomViews
    Org Agenda Day View alt+o a d (global, opt-in; NeoVintageous shift+space) calendar, week, today and the project lists
    Org Todo View every open todo
    Org Filtered Todo View open todos with the tags you type (tagfilter)
    Org: Agenda Query (orgs) the headings an orgs query finds
    Org: Agenda All Tasks (orgs filter AllTasks) the server's AllTasks filter

    Keys marked global, opt-in are in the example global keymap and are off until you copy them into your own keymap: see Keys.

    In the agenda

    Key Command What it does
    enter Org Agenda Goto open the heading
    space Org Agenda Goto Split open the heading in the other group
    < / > Org Agenda Goto Prev / Next Day move the views a day back or on (refetched for that day)
    g Org Agenda Day View rebuild the day view
    s Org Agenda Change Todo change the todo keyword
    , Org Agenda Change Priority change the priority
    t Org Agenda Insert Tag add or remove a tag
    e Org Agenda Insert Effort set the EFFORT property
    a Org Agenda Insert Assign set the ASSIGNED property
    i Org Agenda Insert Id give the heading an ID (a new uuid) if it has none
    c i / c o Org Agenda ClockIn / ClockOut clock in to the entry, clock out
    alt+o f f open the regex filter of a todo list

    With NeoVintageous in command mode t changes the todo keyword and the filter is f f; the other keys are the same.

    Hovering over an entry shows its heading and file.

    Actions happen on the server

    The heading an entry shows lives in some other file, so the actions above are made by the server: it rewrites the file, and the agenda is fetched again and redrawn. Before the change OrgEverywhere saves the file if it is open with unsaved edits (orgsSaveBeforeServerEdits) and checks the heading is still where the agenda found it. If the file changed so much that the heading cannot be told apart from another one with the same title, the action is refused: refresh the agenda and try again.

    What lands on a day

    The server follows org-mode's agenda rules:

    * Dentist <2026-10-14 Wed 09:30>
* TODO Pay the rent
  SCHEDULED: <2026-10-01 Thu +1m>
* TODO Tax return
  DEADLINE: <2026-10-30 Fri -5d>
* Conference
  <2026-10-20 Tue 09:00>--<2026-10-22 Thu 17:00>
    • A plain active timestamp (in the headline or the heading's own text, not a child's and not inside a drawer) is on its day. Inactive [...] stamps never are.
    • A repeater (+1w, ++1w, .+1w alike) is on its base day and every interval after it, never before.
    • A range <a>--<b> is on every day it spans: with its times on the first and last day, all day in between.
    • SCHEDULED is on its day. While it is not done and the day has passed, it is also on today, marked Sched. Nx (N days late), and only today: overdue is a today problem.

    • DEADLINE is on its day. While it is not done it is also on today during its warning period, marked D:@2026-10-30, and after it, marked D: Overdue; on the day itself it says D: Due Today. The warning period is the stamp's own -Nd, else the server's agenda.deadlineWarningDays (default 14; 0 means only its day):

      server:
  agenda:
    deadlineWarningDays: 14
    • A done heading (a done keyword of its own file) is on the exact days its dates name only: no carrying forward, no warnings. The day view leaves done headings out; the week view draws them crossed out.
    • Archived trees (a heading tagged ARCHIVE, or under one) and commented trees (a COMMENT heading and everything under it) are left out, as in org.

    Times are wall clock times on calendar days, so a time zone or a daylight saving change does not move a date. "Today" is the date of the machine running Sublime.

    The views

    A view is drawn from what the server sent and then filtered by the view's own rules and the filters you give it (below).

    View Shows
    Calendar three months around the current day; days with something on them are marked, repeats in another colour
    Week the timed entries of the week, as blocks on an hour scale
    Day the current day hour by hour, a "now" line, then the entries with no time
    Todos open todos that are not projects
    Projects projects
    Not Blocked Projects projects with a NEXT child
    Blocked Projects projects without a NEXT child (stuck)
    Next Tasks projects that are not stuck, each with its NEXT children
    Loose Tasks open todos that are neither a project nor part of one
    Done done headings (filter it: it can be long)
    Clocked headings with clock lines
    Has Status headings with any keyword
    Notes, Meetings, Phone headings with the NOTE, MEETING or PHONE keyword
    OrgsQuery the headings an orgs query finds (see below)

    The calendar and week leave projects out, the day view leaves done and archived headings out.

    What a project is depends on agendaProjectIs: nested_todo (the default: a todo with todo children), tag (a heading tagged PROJECT) or property (a heading with a PROJECT property).

    The day view

    Each line is file: time keyword heading and what the server said about it (Sched. 3x, D:@2026-10-30, D: Overdue). Timed entries sit at their hour; entries that run over several hours are marked down the left so you can see what overlaps. The hours shown are agendaDayStartTime (6) to agendaDayEndTime (19), extended when something is later. A scheduled habit (:STYLE: habit) shows a bar of the last three weeks.

    Custom views

    AgendaCustomViews names lists of views; each list is shown as one agenda. Org Agenda Custom View shows Default, Org Agenda Choose View offers them all.

    "AgendaCustomViews":
{
    "Default": ["Calendar", "Week", "Day", "Blocked Projects", "Next Tasks", "Loose Tasks"],
    "Work":    ["Day : tagfilter +WORK", "Todos : tagfilter +WORK -SOMEDAY : showdate 15.15 : showeffort"],
    "Waiting": ["Todos : statefilter +WAITING : showassigned"],
    "Week done": ["Done : durationfilter -7d : showdate 15.15"],
    "Server":  ["OrgsQuery : query IsTodo() && InTagGroup(\"WORK\") : title Work",
                "OrgsQuery : filter NextTasks"],
},

    Each entry is a view name followed by : argument value or : flag parts. The parts are split on :, so a value cannot contain one.

    Filters

    Every view takes these:

    Todos : tagfilter +WORK -SOMEDAY
Todos : tagfilter |HOME |GARDEN
Todos : priorityfilter |A |B
Todos : statefilter -WAITING
Day   : durationfilter +2d
Done  : durationfilter -30d
Done  : datefilter >=20260101 <20260201
Clocked : clockfilter -7d
    tagfilter
    each word is a tag: +TAG (or just TAG) it must have, -TAG it must not have, and of the |TAG words it must have at least one. Tags are inherited from parents and #+FILETAGS:.
    priorityfilter
    the same with priorities.
    statefilter
    the same with the todo keyword; each word is a regular expression.
    durationfilter
    +2d keeps headings whose scheduled date, deadline or first timestamp is no later than two days from now; -30d drops headings closed more than 30 days ago.
    clockfilter
    keeps headings with clock lines; -7d keeps only those whose every clock line ended in the last 7 days.
    datefilter
    keeps headings closed in a date range, written YYYYMMDD after >, >=, < or <=.

    Durations are written 2d, 3h, 45min, 1y or 1:30.

    Flags: hasschedule, hasdeadline, hasclock, hasclose, noschedule, nodeadline, noclock, noclose, haschildtasks, nochildtasks, clockedtoday, and onlytasks (the calendar, week and day show only todos).

    Columns of the todo lists

    The list views (Todos, Projects, Done…) show file, keyword and heading. More columns are flags, or a flag with a python format width:

    • showdate, showtime, showeffort, showafter (the AFTER property), showassigned (ASSIGNED), showid (ID or CUSTOM_ID), showduration (time clocked) and showtotalduration (a total line). showdate 15.15 gives the date its full width.
    • hidefilename, hidestatus, hideheading.
    • byproject groups the tasks under their project.
    • sortascend / sortdescend (default from agendaTodoSortAscending, ascending).

    A list view has a regex filter on the heading: alt+o f f opens it (agendaTodoFilterByDefault opens it with the view).

    Server queries

    The OrgsQuery view and Org: Agenda Query (orgs) show the headings an orgs query language expression finds (see The Query Language):

    • OrgsQuery : query IsTodo() && HasTags("WORK") runs that query.
    • OrgsQuery : filter NextTasks runs one of the server's named filters (AllTasks, NextTasks, StuckProjects…).
    • : title Work names the view.
    • With neither, agendaOrgsQueryDefault (IsTodo() && !IsArchived()).

    Org: Agenda Query (orgs) offers this session's recent queries, the server's saved queries and its filters; whichever you pick can be edited before it runs. A query that does not parse says why in the view.

    Settings

    Setting Default Effect
    AgendaCustomViews see above the custom views
    agendaSaveBeforeRender false save modified org buffers before fetching the agenda
    firstDayOfWeek "Sunday" first day of the week and the calendar (a day name)
    agendaWeekViewNumDays 7 days in the week view (5 with Monday for a work week)
    agendaDayStartTime 6 first hour of the day and week views
    agendaDayEndTime 19 last hour
    agendaHeaderFormat "%A %d %B %Y" (a tab after the day name) the day view's date heading (strftime)
    agendaProjectIs "nested_todo" what a project is: nested_todo, tag or property
    agendaTodoFilterByDefault false open the regex filter with a list view
    agendaOrgsQueryDefault IsTodo() && !IsArchived() the query of an OrgsQuery view without one

    Notifications

    OrgEverywhere reminds you of today's appointments. A background thread asks the server for today's agenda (and again when the server re-reads a file, and every few checks) and keeps the timed entries that are not done. When one is notifyMinsBefore minutes away it:

    • shows a Notifications view in Sublime with the reminders so far, and
    • runs an outside notification: on macOS osascript (a system notification), on Windows the balloontip.ps1 script that comes with the package.

    Each entry is announced once a day.

    Setting Default Effect
    notifyMinsBefore 15 minutes before the start to remind
    notifyHoursBefore 0 hours, added to the minutes
    noticePeriod 1 minutes between checks (at least 1)
    ExternalNotificationCommand per OS the command line to run; {todo} and {time} are filled in

    Org Agenda Rebuild Notices rebuilds today's list now.

    Capture, Refile and Archive

    Capture

    Capture is for getting a thought out of your head quickly, without leaving what you are doing: press a key, type, close the panel, and it is filed. Most people capture into an inbox and sort it out later with refile.

    Command Keys
    Org Capture ctrl+shift+x, alt+o z (global, opt-in; NeoVintageous command mode: Z)

    The keys are global and opt-in: copy them from the example global keymap (see Keys) to use them.

    Org Capture lists your own templates (the captureTemplates setting) and then, when the orgs server is connected, the server's templates, shown as orgs: Name. The two kinds work differently.

    Server templates

    The server's templates live in its orgs.yaml, so Sublime, worg, the command line and VSCode capture with the same ones:

    server:
  captureTemplates:
    - name: "Todo"
      type: "entry"
      target:
        type: "file+headline"
        filename: "inbox.org"
        id: "Inbox"
      template: |-
        TODO {{Heading}}
        :PROPERTIES:
          :CREATED: {{now}}
        :END:
        {{CONTENT}}

    The template is a form with fields to fill in:

    • {{name}} a value, labelled from its name,
    • {{name|prompt}} the same with your own label,
    • {{name|=default}} pre-filled and still editable (the server fills in uuid, now, username and the like this way),
    • {{CONTENT}} the body.

    OrgEverywhere turns the form into a snippet in the capture panel: each field is a tab stop, defaults are filled in. For an entry the first line is the heading (keyword, priority and :tags: kept) and the rest its content. When the panel loses focus the text is sent to the server once and the panel closes; the server writes the target file (saving its buffer first if it is open with changes). Closing the panel before typing anything sends nothing.

    • Org: Abort Capture (orgs template) throws the capture away instead.
    • If the server does not answer in time the capture may still have been written: you are asked before it is sent again. On any other error the text stays in the panel and is sent next time it loses focus.

    Set orgsCaptureTemplates to false to leave the server's templates out of the list. Org: orgs reload server config re-reads orgs.yaml after you change the templates.

    Local templates

    The captureTemplates setting holds templates that OrgEverywhere files itself, writing the target file directly:

    "refile": "~/notes/refile.org",
"captureTemplates":
[
    { "name": "Todo",    "type": "entry", "snippet": "todo_heading",    "target": ["file", "{refile}"] },
    { "name": "Meeting", "type": "entry", "snippet": "meeting_heading", "target": ["file+headline", "~/notes/work.org", "Meetings"], "openas": "direct" },
    { "name": "Journal", "type": "entry", "snippet": "note_heading",    "target": ["file+olp+datetree", "~/notes/journal.org"] },
],
    name
    the name in the list.
    snippet
    a sublime snippet (without .sublime-snippet) from your Packages/User/orgsnippets folder or the package's own: todo_heading, note_heading, meeting_heading, capture_heading, plain_template.
    type
    entry (a heading under the target), item (a list item in the first list there), checkitem (a checkbox item), table-line (a row of the first table) or plain (text at the end of the target).
    target
    where it goes (below).
    openas
    "panel" (the default: a capture panel, written to the target when it loses focus) or "direct" (opens the target file at the place instead).
    properties
    for a datetree, the heading formats {"year-format": "%Y", "month-format": "%Y-%m %B", "day-format": "%Y-%m-%d %A"}.
    Targets
    Target Goes
    ["file", path] at the end of the file
    ["file+headline", path, "Heading"] under that heading (made if it is missing)
    ["file+olp", path, "Heading 1", "Heading 2"] under the heading at that outline path
    ["file+regexp", path, "regex"] at the first line matching the regular expression
    ["file+olp+datetree", path, "Heading"...] under today's year / month / day headings, made as needed
    ["id", "custom-id"] under the heading with that CUSTOM_ID
    ["clock"] under the heading the clock is running on

    In a path, {refile} is the refile setting and {daypage} is today's local day page (dayPagePath, see Day Pages). A missing target file is created.

    Snippet variables

    Capture snippets can use these besides sublime's own:

    Variable Value
    ORG_INACTIVE_DATE [2026-10-11 Sun]
    ORG_ACTIVE_DATE <2026-10-11 Sun>
    ORG_DATE 2026-10-11
    ORG_TIME 14:05:09
    ORG_CLIPBOARD the clipboard
    ORG_SELECTION the selected text where you captured
    ORG_LINENUM the line you captured from
    ORG_FILENAME the file you captured from

    A snippet that links back to where you were:

    <snippet>
    <content><![CDATA[
* NOTE ${1:HEADING}
  :PROPERTIES:
  :FROM:    [[file:${ORG_FILENAME}::${ORG_LINENUM}][Source]]
  :CREATED: $ORG_INACTIVE_DATE
  :END:
  $0
]]></content>
    <tabTrigger>capture_heading</tabTrigger>
    <scope>text.orgmode</scope>
</snippet>

    captureBufferName names the panel (*capture*) and captureWriteFormat is the encoding the target is written in (utf-8). Org Open Refile (ctrl+alt+x in the example global keymap, see Keys) opens the refile file.

    Refile and copy

    Refile moves the heading at the cursor (and everything under it) to another place; copy leaves the original where it is. The orgs server does it: it offers its refile targets, moves the subtree and rewrites both files. Open buffers of those files are saved first if they have changes, and reload when the server has written them.

    Command Keys Target
    Org Refile alt+o R (NeoVintageous R) any heading, or the end of a file
    Org Refile To EOF NeoVintageous space r f the end of a file
    Org Refile File and Heading NeoVintageous space r r a file, then a heading in it
    Org Copy any heading, or the end of a file

    The list shows each target as KEYWORD Outline / path :tags: with its file, and previews it as you move (orgsPreviewOnHighlight). It goes orgsRefileDepth levels deep (3). Which files are offered is the server's call (its org directories, and its refile settings).

    Archive

    Archiving moves a finished subtree out of the way, into an archive file.

    Command What it does
    Org Archive Subtree archive the heading at the cursor
    Org Archive All Done archive every done heading in this file, in one request
    Org Insert Archive Tag tag the heading ARCHIVE: it stays where it is, archived

    The server archives, to the first of:

    1. the heading's ARCHIVE property,
    2. the file's #+ARCHIVE: line,
    3. the server's archiveDefault in orgs.yaml (default %s_archive::, org's own: notes.org archives to notes.org_archive).

    %s is the file's name; after :: comes the heading to file under (nothing: the top level).

    #+ARCHIVE: %s_archive::* Archived Tasks
* DONE Old project
  :PROPERTIES:
  :ARCHIVE: ~/notes/archive/2026.org::
  :END:

    The old archive setting is not read any more. Keep .org_archive in validOrgExtensions so archive files open as org. A tree tagged ARCHIVE in place is left out of the agenda.

    Clocking

    Clocking time

    Org can record how long you work on a task: clock in when you start, clock out when you stop, and a CLOCK: line with the start, end and duration goes into the heading's :LOGBOOK: drawer:

    * TODO Write the report
  :LOGBOOK:
  CLOCK: [2026-10-11 Sun 09:02]--[2026-10-11 Sun 10:47] =>  1:45
  :END:

    Together with effort estimates (EFFORT property, Org Insert Effort) and clock reports it shows where your time went and how your estimates held up, and it makes timesheets easy.

    Command Keys What it does
    Org Clock In alt+o c i (NeoVintageous space c i) start the clock on this heading
    Org Clock Out alt+o c o (NeoVintageous space c o) stop the clock
    Org Jump To Clock open the heading the clock is on
    Org Agenda ClockIn / Out c i / c o in the agenda clock in to an agenda entry, out
    Org: orgs Clock Report time clocked across all files

    The clock lives on the server

    With the orgs server connected, the clock is the server's. There is one running clock for all your orgs clients: clock in from Sublime and worg shows it running; clock out from the command line and Sublime's status bar stops. Starting a clock stops the one already running.

    • Clocking in tells the server; nothing is written to the file yet.
    • Clocking out has the server write the CLOCK: line into the heading's :LOGBOOK:. If that file is open with unsaved changes it is saved first; the buffer reloads with the new line.
    • The server can also stop the clock by itself (its autoclockout plugin). OrgEverywhere hears of clock changes through the server's events and looks again every orgsClockPollSeconds (120).

    Org files show the running clock in the status bar, Clock: Write the report (1:45), unless clockShowInStatus is false. Org Jump To Clock asks the server where the clock is and opens the heading.

    Org Clear Clock and Org Update Active Clock only apply to the offline clock: a server clock is stopped with clock out, and has no open CLOCK: line in the file to read a start time back from.

    Without a server

    When no server is connected the old local clock is used: clocking in writes an open CLOCK: [start]-- line into the heading's logbook and remembers the clock in Packages/User/OrgEverywhere_Clocks.yaml; clocking out closes the line and saves the file. This clock is Sublime's alone.

    • clockingSubMinuteClocks (true): keep clock lines shorter than a minute; false removes them on clock out.
    • clockInPropertyBlock (false): write CLOCK into the property drawer instead of the logbook.

    A clock started offline is closed the offline way when you next clock in or out with the server connected (the server does not know about it).

    Org Recalculate Clock rewrites the clock lines of the heading at the cursor, recomputing their durations.

    Clock reports

    Org: orgs Clock Report asks which period (today, yesterday, this week, last week, this month, last month, this year, last year, everything until now) and shows a table of the time clocked in every file, by heading, with the total:

    #+TITLE: Clock report: This week
Total: 12:30   (6 entries)

| Headline            | File      |  Time |
|---------------------+-----------+-------|
| Website             | work.org  |  8:15 |
| \_ Write the report | work.org  |  1:45 |
...

    enter or a double click on a row opens that heading, g refreshes.

    Inside a file, a clocktable dynamic block sums the clocks of the subtree it is in; Org: orgs Update Dynamic Blocks has the server refresh the dynamic blocks of a file (see the tables and dynamic blocks guides).

    Clocking or today?

    Clocking is not for everyone. If you do not need the minutes, keeping a "today" heading or a day page gives you most of the benefit with less ceremony: see Markers and Today and Day Pages.

    Day Pages

    A page a day

    A day page is a work log: one org file per day (or per week), named by its date, that you open in the morning, plan the day in, and write notes, meetings and progress into as the day goes. Yesterday's page is a keypress away.

    Command Keys What it does
