    Org Day Page Create alt+o d c (global, opt-in; NeoVintageous space d c) open today's page, making it if needed
    Org Day Page Previous alt+o d p (NeoVintageous space d p) the page before the one you are on
    Org Day Page Next alt+o d n (NeoVintageous space d n) the page after; past the last one, today's page

    alt+o d c is global and opt-in: copy it from the example global keymap (see Keys) to use it.

    Previous and next step from the page you are looking at (or from today) to the nearest page that exists.

    Day pages from the server

    When the orgs server has a dayPagePath its day pages are used, the same ones worg and the orgs command line open:

    server:
  dayPagePath: "/Users/me/notes/worklog"
  dayPageMode: "week"          # or "day"
  dayPageModeWeekDay: "Monday"
  dayPageTemplate: "daypage.tpl"

    The server names the pages (Mon_2026_10_12.org), makes today's page from its template, and when it does, carries the open tasks over from the last page and archives it. In week mode there is one page per week, named by dayPageModeWeekDay, and previous / next step a week.

    Today's tasks

    When today's page is new, OrgEverywhere adds today's open tasks from your other files to it: what the server's agenda has on today (scheduled, carried forward because it is overdue, deadlines due or warning, dated today) that is a todo, not done and not archived. Each is copied with its text up to its first child heading; a task already on the page (the server may have carried it over) is not copied again, nor is a child of a task that is. Set dayPageCopyTasksForToday to false to turn this off.

    Local day pages

    Without a server, or when the server has no dayPagePath, OrgEverywhere makes the pages itself from its own settings (the status bar says it is using them):

    Setting Default Effect
    dayPagePath not set the folder for day pages (a string)
    dayPageNameFormat "%a_%Y_%m_%d" strftime name of a page; old pages are found by it, so keep it
    dayPageMode "day" "week" for a page per week
    dayPageModeWeekDay "Monday" the day a week page is named by
    dayPageSnippet "dayPageSnippet" the snippet a new page starts with (orgsnippets folder)
    dayPageArchiveOld true tag the previous page #+FILETAGS: ARCHIVE when a new one is made
    dayPageCopyOpenTasks true copy the previous page's open top level tasks to the new one
    dayPageCopyTasksForToday true add today's tasks from other files (needs the server)
    dayPageCreateOldPages false Previous makes the page for the day before if it is missing

    The day page snippet gets the capture snippet variables (ORG_ACTIVE_DATE, ORG_DATE…) plus ORG_AUTHOR, and ORG_FILENAME is the page's date name.

    A capture template can target today's local page with {daypage} (see Capture, Refile and Archive).

    Markers and Today

    Markers

    A marker is a tag that only one heading carries at a time. Putting it on a heading takes it off whichever heading had it before. The orgs server keeps markers, so every client finds the same heading.

    Command What it does
    Org Set Today put the today marker on the heading at the cursor
    Org: Set Marker pick a marker from orgsMarkers and put it here
    Org: Jump To Marker pick a marker and open the heading that carries it
    Org Jump To Today open the heading that carries the today marker
    Org Link To Today link this heading from today's heading and schedule it 
      "orgsTodayMarker": "TODAY",
  "orgsMarkers": ["TODAY", "FOCUS"],

    orgsMarkers lists the markers the commands offer (the today marker is always among them); with only one there is nothing to pick.

    Today

    "Today" is the heading carrying the orgsTodayMarker marker (TODAY). It is meant for a work log: each morning start a heading for the day (or open your day page) and Org Set Today on it. From then on:

    • Org Jump To Today takes you back to it from anywhere.
    • Org Link To Today on a task schedules the task for now (so it is on today's agenda), then adds a child heading under today with a link back to the task. Your log lists what you meant to do; the agenda tracks it.
    * 2026-10-11 Sunday                                            :TODAY:
** Write the report
   [[file:~/notes/work.org::*Write the report][Write the report]]

    Before markers, today was the heading with :CUSTOM_ID: TODAY. When no heading carries the marker that heading is still found.

    Moving the marker edits two files (the old holder loses the tag, the new one gets it). The server makes those edits, saving open buffers with changes first.

    A GTD Workflow

    Getting Things Done in org

    Org lets you organise yourself however you like; one popular way is David Allen's Getting Things Done. GTD needs a handful of tools, and each has an org equivalent in OrgEverywhere:

    GTD In OrgEverywhere
    the inbox a capture template into inbox.org
    the calendar scheduled items, deadlines and timestamps on the agenda
    projects todos with todo children (agendaProjectIs)
    next actions the NEXT keyword, the Next Tasks view
    waiting for the WAITING keyword, a statefilter view
    someday / maybe a someday.org file, or a SOMEDAY tag
    contexts tags (@home, @phone) and tag groups
    reference plain headings, links and ids, full text search
    daily and weekly review the agenda, refile, archive, Blocked Projects

    This is one way of doing it; take what helps.

    Capture everything

    The first rule is to get things out of your head into a place you trust, fast enough that you never put it off. Put a capture template on a key and send everything to one inbox:

    server:
  captureTemplates:
    - name: "Inbox"
      type: "entry"
      target:
        type: "file"
        filename: "inbox.org"
      template: |-
        TODO {{What}}
        :PROPERTIES:
          :CREATED: {{now}}
        :END:
        {{CONTENT}}

    Because it is a server template, the same capture works from worg on your phone and from the command line. Org Capture, pick orgs: Inbox, type, move on. See Capture, Refile and Archive.

    Context comes from tags: :@work:, :@home:, :@phone:. Put a tag on a whole file with #+FILETAGS: (#+FILETAGS: :work: at the top of work.org) and everything in it inherits it.

    The daily review

    Each morning, empty the inbox:

    1. Open inbox.org and go through it from the top.
    2. Two minutes or less? Do it, mark it DONE.
    3. Otherwise Org Refile (alt+o R) it to the project it belongs to, or to someday.org, or Org Archive Subtree it if it needs nothing.
    4. Give actions a NEXT keyword when they are the next thing to do on their project, a SCHEDULED date if they belong to a day, a DEADLINE if they have one.

    Then plan the day: open the agenda (Org Agenda Custom View). The day view shows what is fixed today, what is overdue ("Sched. 3x"), and deadlines coming up. With a "today" heading (see Markers and Today) or a day page (see Day Pages) you can list the tasks you mean to do and keep notes as you go.

    Projects and next actions

    In GTD a project is anything that takes more than one action. With the default agendaProjectIs of nested_todo, a todo with todo children is a project:

    * TODO Move house                                             :@home:
** DONE Get three quotes from movers
** NEXT Book the movers
** TODO Change the address at the bank

    A project with a NEXT child is moving; one without is stuck. The agenda's views split them:

    • Next Tasks lists the moving projects with their NEXT actions: this is your list of what to do now.
    • Blocked Projects lists the stuck ones: each needs a next action.
    • Loose Tasks lists the todos that belong to no project, where things get lost.

    The default agenda shows all three under the calendar, week and day.

    Deciding what to do

    1. The agenda's day: what has to happen today.

    2. Then the next actions for the context you are in. A custom view per context:

      "AgendaCustomViews":
{
    "Default": ["Calendar", "Week", "Day", "Blocked Projects", "Next Tasks", "Loose Tasks"],
    "@work":   ["Day : tagfilter +@work", "Todos : statefilter +NEXT : tagfilter +@work"],
    "@home":   ["Todos : statefilter +NEXT : tagfilter +@home"],
    "Waiting": ["Todos : statefilter +WAITING : showassigned : showdate 15.15"],
},

    Or with the server's query language, which can also use tag groups (tagGroups in orgs.yaml, so HOME can mean @home and @garden):

       "Work next": ["OrgsQuery : query IsNextTask() && !InTagGroup(\"HOME\") : title Work next"],

    The server ships filters for these questions (NextTasks, StuckProjects, LooseTasks, WorkTasks, HomeTasks…): Org: Agenda Query (orgs) lists them.

    The weekly review

    Once a week, look at everything:

    • Blocked Projects: give every stuck project a next action.
    • The Waiting view: chase what you are waiting for.
    • someday.org: promote anything whose time has come.
    • Org Archive All Done in each project file to put finished work away.
    • Org: orgs Habits to see how your routines are going.
    • Org: orgs Clock Report for last week, if you clock.

    worg has Inbox and Weekly Review tabs built on the server's review: settings (Org: orgs Open Web UI).

    Everywhere

    A trusted system has to be with you. The orgs server is what makes the same files available everywhere: worg in a browser (and on a phone), VSCode, the orgs command line and Sublime all see the same agenda, clock and inbox. Keep the org directory in git as well: Org: orgs File History then shows how any file looked at any commit.

    Links

    Links between files and headings, ids, backlinks and images.

    Links

    Writing links

    A link is a pair of square brackets holding a target and, optionally, a description. Org shows the description and hides the target:

    [[https://orgmode.org][The org mode site]]
[[file:projects.org][Projects]]
[[id:6f1c2d0e-1f6a-4c43-9b0e-3a7f3e0f9d12][The budget review]]

    Typing <l and tab expands the link snippet. enter on a link (or Org Open Link) follows it.

    Link types

    Link Goes to
    https://..., http://... the browser
    file:notes.org the file (relative to this one, or absolute; ~ works)
    file:notes.org::42 line 42 (::42::7 adds a column)
    file:notes.org::*Heading the heading with that title in that file
    file:notes.org::#custom-id the heading with that CUSTOM_ID (or ID)
    file:notes.org::text a <<target>>, a #+NAME:, or a heading of that title
    id:UUID the heading with that ID (or CUSTOM_ID), in any file
    #custom-id the heading with that CUSTOM_ID (or ID)
    *Heading the heading with that title in this file
    text a <<target>>, a #+NAME: or a heading in this file
    mailto:me@example.com, email: the mail program (email:me@x.com/Subject adds a subject)
    cmd:path, prompt:path a terminal at that path
    jira:ABC-123 see Links the server knows

    Files that are not org or text (*.pdf, *.docx…) open in their own program. resolver.local_file.force_into_sublime lists the patterns that always open in Sublime, and file_exclude_patterns the ones that never do.

    Targets

    A target is an anchor in the text, written in double angle brackets. A link with its text jumps to it:

    <<budget-notes>>
...
[[budget-notes][see the budget notes]]
[[file:work.org::budget-notes][from another file]]

    Ids and the server

    A heading can carry an :ID: (a uuid, Org Create Heading Id) or a :CUSTOM_ID: of your choosing (Org Insert CustomId, alt+o i i). Ids keep a link working when the heading moves to another file or is renamed, which a *Heading link does not.

    The orgs server knows every id in every file, so id: and #custom-id links (also file:x.org::#custom-id) are looked up there and land on the heading wherever it now is. A heading whose buffer has moved it since the last save is found at its place in the buffer, and an id only in an unsaved buffer is still found in the open buffers.

    *Heading and plain text links are read from the file itself: its buffer when it is open, the file on disk otherwise.

    Org Jump To CustomId lists every custom id the server knows and opens the one you pick.

    Making links

    • Org Create Link (alt+o y l from the example global keymap, see Keys; NeoVintageous space y l) puts a link to where the cursor is on the clipboard: to the <<target>> or #+NAME: on the line, else to the heading (by its ID or CUSTOM_ID if it has one, else by its title), else to the line. Outside org files it links to the line and column.
    • Org Link To File lists the org files the server knows, with their #+TITLE: (and #+ROAM_TAGS:), and inserts a link to the one you pick, described by its title. insertRoamTagToFileLink (true) keeps the roam tags in the description; linkFindUseRoamTags (true) shows them in the list.

    Finding links

    Backlinks

    Backlinks are the links in other files that point at this one: the other direction of a link, as in org-roam.

    • Org Show Backlinks opens a Backlinks view for the current file: the linking files, each link with its line and outline path, and (broken) on a link that no longer resolves. Each entry is a link: enter follows it. While it is showing, the view follows the org file you switch to and updates when files change (backlinksUpdate).
    • Org Jump To Backlink lists them in a quick panel and opens the one you pick.

    The server works out the links, so a backlink only counts once its file is saved.

    Searching all links

    Org Search Links lists every link in every org file (description, target, file, line and heading) and previews each as you move through the list. Handy when you know you linked to something, somewhere.

    Links the server knows

    The server can teach links new protocols in its orgs.yaml:

    server:
  linkProtocols:
    jira:
      urlPrefix: "https://mycompany.atlassian.net/browse/"
    wiki:
      url: "https://wiki.example.com/pages/{{path}}/view"
    ticket:
      cmd: "tkt show"

    A link whose protocol OrgEverywhere does not handle itself (anything but file, id, http, https, mailto, email, cmd, prompt and jira) is sent to the server, which says where it goes:

    • a web url opens in the browser;
    • any other kind of url asks you first ("The orgs server resolved … Open it?");
    • a command always asks before it runs ("The orgs server wants to run this command for the link … Run it?"), and runs in the folder of the file holding the link.

    If the server does not know the protocol the local resolvers get it. jira: goes to the server too unless you have set resolver.jira.url (with resolver.jira.pattern) for the local jira resolver.

    linkResolvers lists the local resolvers and their order (internal, http, https, prompt, jira, email, file); your own resolver modules go in Packages/User/orgresolver.

    Images

    An image link can be shown in the buffer, under the link. It is drawn with a phantom, so it is not text and does not change line numbers.

    Command What it does
    Org Show Images show every image link in the file
    Org Hide Images hide them
    Org Show Image show the image link at the cursor
    Org Hide Image hide it

    #+STARTUP: inlineimages shows a file's images when it opens; the startup setting (default ["showall", "noinlineimages"]) does it for every file.

    Images on the web are downloaded into a cache the first time they are shown, which can make Sublime wait: turn inline images on with care. A relative image path is looked for next to the file, then in the imageSearchPath folders.

    Tables

    Tables, the formula language, plots, the column view and dynamic blocks.

    Tables and Spreadsheets

    Tables in a plain text file

    An org table is a block of lines that start with |. OrgEverywhere keeps it aligned as you type, lets you move rows and columns around and runs formulas over it, so a table can be a small spreadsheet that lives in your notes.

    Emacs evaluates table formulas with calc and emacs lisp. OrgEverywhere has its own formula language instead: the cell reference syntax of org (@2$3, $1..$3, @>) on top of python style expressions, with a set of spreadsheet functions. Most simple org formulas work unchanged; calc specific functions and lisp formulas ('(...)) do not.

    The editing half (alignment, moving cells, inserting rows and columns) comes from the Table Editor package, which OrgEverywhere installs and turns on for org files (enable_table_editor, table_editor_syntax).

    Tables are part of the file you are editing: everything here works on the buffer, with or without the orgs server. Only references to tables in other files (remote references by id, random rows from any table) ask the server where those tables are.

    Creating a table

    Type a |, some text and press tab: the line becomes a table row and the cursor moves to the next cell. Type |- on the next line and press tab to turn it into a separator (hline).

      | Name  | Qty | Price |
  |-------+-----+-------|
  | Apple |   3 |  0.50 |
  | Pear  |   2 |  0.75 |

    Other ways to get a table:

    • Org Insert Blank Table (org_insert_blank_table) asks for the size as WxH (4x3) and inserts an empty table with a header separator.
    • Org Convert Region To Table (org_convert_selection_to_table) turns the selected text into a table. The separator is guessed from the text: comma, semicolon, tab or space, whichever splits the lines most evenly (comma wins a tie). A python style list of lists ([[1,2],[3,4]]) is understood too.
    • Org Import Csv (org_import_table_from_csv) asks for a file and inserts its contents as a table at the cursor, with the same separator guessing.

    Editing a table

    tab and shift+tab move between cells and realign the table, enter moves down a row. The rest of the editing keys:

    Keys Does
    tab / shift+tab next / previous cell (and align)
    enter next row
    shift+enter split the cell: the text after the cursor moves down
    alt+shift+right insert a column
    alt+shift+left delete the column
    alt+shift+down insert a row
    alt+shift+up delete the row
    alt+right / alt+left move the column right / left
    alt+up / alt+down move the row up / down
    alt+o t a align the table
    alt+o t - insert a separator line
    alt+o t = insert a double separator line
    alt+o enter separator below, and move past it
    alt+o t j join the current line with the next

    With NeoVintageous the same commands sit under space in command mode (space t a, space t -, space t e …).

    Moving or inserting rows and columns also updates the formulas below the table, so a formula that read $3 reads the column's new number. A formula that pointed at a deleted row or column is marked @INVALID or $INVALID so you can see it needs fixing.

    Org Clear Table Cell (org_clear_cell, space t k) empties the cell under the cursor.

    Formulas

    Writing a formula

    Formulas live on a #+TBLFM: line directly under the table. Each formula has a target and an expression; several formulas share the line, separated by ::.

      | Name  | Qty | Price | Total |
  |-------+-----+-------+-------|
  | Apple |   3 |  0.50 |   1.5 |
  | Pear  |   2 |  0.75 |   1.5 |
  |-------+-----+-------+-------|
  | Sum   |   5 |       |   3.0 |
  #+TBLFM:$4=$2*$3::@>$2=vsum(@2..@-1)::@>$4=vsum(@2..@-1)

    You do not have to edit the #+TBLFM: line by hand. Type the formula into a cell and evaluate the table: OrgEverywhere moves it to the #+TBLFM: line, with a target made from the cell you typed it in.

    You type It becomes Applies to
    =$2*$3 $4=$2*$3 the whole column
    :=$2*$3 @3$4=$2*$3 this cell only
    >=vsum($2..$4) @3=vsum($2..$4) the whole row

    If the cell already has a formula, the new one replaces it.

    Evaluating
    • alt+o c c (org_recalc, space c c with NeoVintageous) in a table evaluates every formula of that table. org_recalc is the do what I mean key: on a source block it runs the block, on a dynamic block it refreshes the block, in a table it recalculates.
    • Org Eval Cell (org_fill_in_formula_from_cell) does the same from a cell, after moving a formula typed into the cell to #+TBLFM:.
    • Org Execute Formula (org_execute_formula) evaluates only the formula of the cell under the cursor.
    • Org Execute All Tables (org_execute_all_tables) recalculates every table in the file, top to bottom.

    A formula that fails writes <ERR> into its cells; the python console (ctrl+`) has the details.

    Seeing what a formula touches

    When the cursor is in a cell that a formula writes, the cells the formula reads are outlined, and so is the formula on the #+TBLFM: line. With the cursor on a formula in the #+TBLFM: line, the same happens for that formula.

    • Org Show Table Rows / Org Hide Table Rows put the row and column numbers next to the table, which helps when writing references. Separator lines are numbered with roman numerals.
    • Org Highlight Formula (org_highlight_formula) highlights the formula under the cursor; Org Clear Table Highlights (org_clear_table_regions) removes the outlines.
    • tableShowCursor (default true) outlines the cell under the cursor. A NoTableHighlight property on the heading turns the outlines off for its tables.
    Changing a formula

    Org Edit Table Formula (org_edit_formula_for_cell, space t e) copies the formula of the current cell back into the cell. Edit it and evaluate the table again.

    Note that the copy carries its full target ($4=$2*$3). Put the leading marker back (=, :=, >=) to say how the formula should be stored, or edit the #+TBLFM: line directly.

    A one off formula over a column

    Org Table Exec Below (org_exec_on_column) asks for an expression and applies it once to the current cell and every cell below it in the column. Nothing is stored. Useful for nudging a column of numbers: $0*1.1.

    The formula language

    References

    Rows and columns are numbered from 1. Separator lines are not counted: in the table above, @1 is the header row and @2 is "Apple".

    Reference Means
    @2$3 row 2, column 3
    $3 column 3 of the row being computed
    @2 row 2 of the column being computed
    $-1, $+2 one column left, two columns right of the current one
    @-1, @+1 the row above, the row below
    @-1$-2 relative row and column together
    @<, @<< the first row, the second row
    @>, @>> the last row, the last but one
    $<, $> the first column, the last column
    @#, $# the number of the current row, of the current column
    $1..$3 columns 1 to 3 of the current row (a range)
    @2..@-1 rows 2 to the one above, in the current column
    @2$1..@4$3 the block of cells between the two corners

    Org's @I / @II references to separator lines are not supported.

    Targets

    The part before the = says which cells the formula fills.

    Target Fills
    $4= column 4, every row below the first separator
    @3= row 3, every column
    @3$4= one cell
    @>$2= the last row, column 2
    @2$1..@5$2= every cell of the block
    $name= a named column (see Advanced tables)

    A column formula skips the rows above the first separator, so headers are safe. A single cell formula wins over a column or row formula that covers the same cell.

    Expressions

    Expressions are python expressions evaluated in a sandbox: + - * /, % (modulo), ** (power), comparisons (== != < > <= >=), and, or, not, strings in quotes and the conditional form:

      $4=$2*$3 if $3 > 0 else 0
  $5="late" if date($4) < now() else ""

    A cell's text becomes a value when it is used: 12 and 1.5 are numbers, 40% is 0.4, true, t and false are booleans, anything else is a string. Dates and durations need date() and duration().

    Format flags

    A formula can end in ;flags:

    • N - empty cells count as 0 (normally an empty cell is an empty string, and adding it to a number fails).
    • %.2f - print floating point results with that many decimals.
      | a     | b     | c   |
  | 1     | 1     |     |
  | 0.476 | 0.476 | 0.0 |
  #+TBLFM:@3=@2/2.1;N%.3f

    The rest of calc's mode flags have no meaning here and are ignored.

    Constants and properties

    #+CONSTANTS: defines names for numbers, used with a $ in front:

      #+CONSTANTS: c=299792458 g=9.81
  | mass | energy |
  |------+--------|
  |    2 |        |
  #+TBLFM:$2=$1*$c**2

    The properties of the heading the table sits under are available the same way, prefixed with PROP_: a heading with :Rate: 85 in its property drawer can use $PROP_Rate in its tables.

    Built in symbols are used without a $: pi, True=/=true=/=t, False=/=false, None=/=nil.

    Functions
    Function Does
    vsum(range) sum of the cells
    vmean(range) average
    vmedian(range) median
    vmax(range), vmin(range) largest, smallest
    vsumifeq(a,b,range) sum of the cells of range on rows where a == b
    vsumifgt, vsumiflt, vsumifgteq, vsumiflteq the same with >, <, >=, <=
    abs, int, float, bool, str conversions
    round, floor, ceil, trunc rounding
    sqrt, pow(x,y), exp, log, log10, log2 math
    sin, cos, tan, asin, acos, atan trigonometry (radians)
    sinh, cosh, tanh, asinh, acosh, atanh hyperbolic functions
    degrees, radians convert angles
    rand(), randomf() random number from 0 to 1
    random(a,b), randint(n) random integer from a to b, below n
    now() the current date and time
    date(x) an org timestamp from a cell or string
    duration(x) a duration (3d, 2h, 1:30); add it to a date
    year, month, day, hour, minute, second parts of a date
    weekday(d), yearday(d) day of the week (monday is 0), day of the year
    time(d) the time of day of a date
    filename(x) a file link or relative path made absolute
    remote(name,@r$c) a cell of another table (see below)
    sbe(name, x=1) the result of a named source block (see Source Blocks)
    highlight(cell,color,text) colour a cell, return text
    red(cell), green, blue, yellow, cyan, purple, pink colour the cell, keep its value
    gradient(cell,pct,c1,c2,...) colour by a 0 to 100 value through a list of colours
    passed(test) a green PASSED or a red FAILED (used by the table tests)

    Dates and durations work together: date($3)+duration($2) is the timestamp $2 after $3.

      | Task   | Effort | Start            | End              |
  |--------+--------+------------------+------------------|
  | Design | 2d     | <2021-03-15 Mon> | <2021-03-17 Wed> |
  | Build  | 4d     | <2021-03-17 Wed> | <2021-03-21 Sun> |
  #+TBLFM:$4=date($3)+duration($2)

    Org Show Table Tests opens the table unit tests: a file of small tables exercising every function, a good place to see a function used.

    Remote references

    remote(name, @r$c) reads a cell of another table. name is either

    • the #+NAME: of a table in the same file, or
    • the ID or CUSTOM_ID of a heading anywhere in your org files: the first table under that heading is used.
      #+NAME: rates
  | role | rate |
  |------+------|
  | dev  |   85 |
  | qa   |   60 |

  | hours | cost |
  |-------+------|
  |    10 |  850 |
  #+TBLFM:$2=$1*remote('rates',@2$2)

    Since 2.0 an id is looked up through the orgs server, so a remote table can be in any file the server knows, open or not (an open buffer is used as is, unsaved changes included). The answer is remembered until the server reports a change, so recalculating a big table does not ask for the same id again and again. Without a server only ids in open buffers are found. A reference that cannot be resolved gives <UNK REF>.

    Advanced tables

    Org's advanced table syntax is supported. Put a marker in the first column of a row. Once a table uses markers, column formulas and row ranges leave the marker column alone; columns keep their numbers, so the first data column is still $2.

    Marker Row is
    ! column names: $a refers to the column named a
    ^ names for the cells in the row above
    _ names for the cells in the row below
    $ parameters: max=5 defines $max for the formulas
    # recalculated as you move through it with tab / enter
    * recalculated with the table, not on the fly
    / skipped by formulas 
      |   | results |    |   |   |   |
  |---+---------+----+---+---+---|
  | ! | a       | b  | c | d | e |
  | # | 9       |    |   | 4 | 5 |
  | # | 3       | 1  | 2 |   |   |
  | $ | max=5   |    |   |   |   |
  | # | 15      | 10 |   |   |   |
  #+TBLFM:@4$2=$b+$c::@3$2=$e+$d::@6$2=$max+$b

    See Advanced features in the org manual.

    Your own functions and symbols

    Python files in Packages/User/orgtable/ can add functions and symbols to the formula language. Turn the folder on first:

      "enableTableExtensions": true,

    • A function: the file name is the function name, the file defines Execute. Packages/User/orgtable/stamp.py gives stamp():

        import datetime

  def Execute():
      return str(datetime.datetime.now())

      Arguments are passed as written in the formula. A cell reference arrives as a cell object: str(cell) is its text.

    • Symbols: a file with AddSymbols(s) adds names to the dictionary it is given. Symbols are used without a $:

        def AddSymbols(s):
      s['c'] = 299792458

    Extensions are loaded once. While writing one set forceLoadExternalExtensions to true so each evaluation reloads them (and turn it off again: it is slow).

    A file of physical constants

    This is the emacs constants.el table as a symbols file. Save it as Packages/User/orgtable/constants.py and formulas can use AU, lyr, kmh, NA and the rest.

    Two names are changed from constants.el: in (inch) is a python keyword and cannot be used in an expression, so it is inch; and t (metric ton) would replace the built in t (true), so it is ton.

      def AddSymbols(s):
      # Natural constants
      s["e"]    = 1.602176462e-19  # Elementary charge [C]
      s["c"]    = 2.99792458e8     # Speed of light [m/s]

    Plotting with gnuplot

    Org Plot Table (org_plot_table) draws a table with gnuplot and puts a link to the picture under the table.

    1. Install gnuplot and tell OrgEverywhere where it is:

        "gnuplot": "/usr/local/bin/gnuplot",
    2. Describe the plot with a #+PLOT: line above the table.
    3. Run Org Plot Table with the cursor in the table (or on the #+PLOT: line).
      #+PLOT: title:"Citations" ind:1 deps:(3 4) with:lines set:grid file:plot.png
  |    Sede   |  Max   | H-index |  top  |
  |-----------+--------+---------+-------|
  | Sao Paolo |  71.00 |   11.50 |  13.5 |
  | Stockholm | 134.19 |   14.33 | 16.33 |
  | Leeds     | 165.77 |   19.68 | 21.68 |
  | Morelia   | 257.56 |   17.67 | 19.67 |
  | Chile     | 257.72 |   21.39 | 23.39 |
  #+TBLFM:$4=$3+2.0

    Option Meaning
    title:"..." the plot title (default "Table Data")
    ind:N the column used as the x axis
    deps:(a b) the columns plotted against it (default: all)
    with:STYLE gnuplot style: lines, points, histograms, candlesticks …
    set:"..." a gnuplot set command; repeat for more
    unset:"..." a gnuplot unset command
    using:"..." a gnuplot using clause, written as is
    include:header plot the rows above the first separator too
    file:NAME the output; the extension picks the terminal (png, jpg, gif, svg, ps, html, txt). file:viewer opens gnuplot's own window instead

    Without file: the picture is plot_<date>_<time>.png beside the org file. The link goes into a #+RESULTS: under the table and the images in the file are shown inline.

    The #+PLOT: line is read from the heading the table sits under: one plot description per heading.

    A gnuplot source block is the other way to plot: see Diagrams.

    Random rows

    Org Insert Rnd Table Row (org_insert_random_row_from_table) picks a named table and inserts one of its rows, chosen at random, at the cursor: a quick way to keep a list of writing prompts, meals or names. Header rows, separators and advanced table marker rows are never picked.

    With the orgs server connected the list offers every #+NAME: table the server knows (plus the ones in this file) and the table can live in any file. Without it only the tables named in this file are offered. A key binding of your own can name the table directly with the tblName argument:

      { "keys": ["ctrl+alt+r"], "command": "org_insert_random_row_from_table",
    "args": { "tblName": "meals" } }

    Tables as data

    A named table can be the input of a source block (:var data=name), and a source block's output can be a table (:results table). See Babel. That makes it easy to turn a table into any other format: a python block that prints csv, for instance.

      #+BEGIN_SRC python :var DATA=prices :results raw
    for r in DATA:
        print(",".join([str(x) for x in r]))
  #+END_SRC

    Column View

    Properties as a table

    Column view shows headings as the rows of a table and their properties as its columns: the effort, owner and state of every task of a project at a glance.

    Emacs draws column view as an overlay on the outline. Sublime cannot, so OrgEverywhere offers the two other ways org has of getting that table:

    • the columnview dynamic block, which writes the table into the file (below), and
    • the orgs web ui's column view: Org: orgs Open Web UI and pick Column View (needs the orgs server; see the orgs Server section).

    Choosing the columns

    #+COLUMNS: lists the columns, in org's format %[WIDTH]PROPERTY[(TITLE)]:

      #+COLUMNS: %40ITEM(Task) %Effort(Effort) %TODO %DEADLINE %TAGS %PRIORITY

    A #+COLUMNS: line applies to the heading it sits under and everything below it; one at the top of the file applies to the whole file. Without one the columns are %70ITEM(Task) %17Effort(Effort).

    Any property name can be a column (%Owner, %Effort). The lookup tries the name as written, then upper and lower case. These special names come from the heading itself:

    Column Value
    ITEM the heading text
    TODO the todo keyword
    PRIORITY the priority letter
    TAGS the heading's own tags
    ALLTAGS its tags including inherited ones
    SCHEDULED the scheduled timestamp
    DEADLINE the deadline timestamp
    CLOSED when it was closed
    TIMESTAMP the first active timestamp in the entry
    TIMESTAMP_IA the first inactive timestamp in the entry
    FILE the name of the file

    The width is accepted and ignored (the table is aligned to its contents). Summary types ({+}, {:}…) and the CLOCKSUM, CATEGORY and BLOCKED columns are not computed.

    The columnview block

      #+BEGIN: columnview :id global :indent t :maxdepth 2 :exclude-tags (Skip)
  #+END:

    Put the cursor on the #+BEGIN: line and press alt+o c c (or run Org Exec Dynamic Block): everything between the two lines is replaced by the table.

      #+BEGIN: columnview :hlines nil :id global :indent t :maxdepth 2
  | Task                       | Effort | Todo | Deadline             | Tags  |
  | 1.1.26                     |        |      |                      | a     |
  | ..Source Blocks            | 2d     | DONE |                      | a     |
  | ..Folding                  |        |      |                      | a     |
  | ..Properties               | 2d     |      | 2021-03-09 Tue 20:55 | a     |
  | ..ColumnView Dynamic Block | 1d     |      |                      | a     |
  #+END:
    Parameter Meaning
    :id global every heading of this file (the default)
    :id local the headings under the top level heading the block sits in
    :id file:NAME every heading of another org file, found by the orgs server
    :id SOME-ID the headings under the heading with that ID or CUSTOM_ID
    :maxdepth N only N levels deep (0, the default, is all of them)
    :indent t indent ITEM with .. per level
    :hlines t a separator before every row; :hlines N before rows up to level N
    :skip-empty-rows t leave out headings whose columns are all empty
    :exclude-tags (A B) leave out headings with any of these tags

    :match (a tags/properties match) is not supported.

    Since 2.0 :id file: and an id are resolved by the orgs server, so the heading or file can be anywhere in your org files, open or not. Without a server only open buffers are found and the block says NO COLUMNVIEW DATA.

    Formulas on a column view

    The block is rewritten each time it runs, so a #+TBLFM: inside it would be lost. Put the #+TBLFM: line directly after #+END: instead: OrgEverywhere treats it as the table's formula line, and it survives a refresh. Columns that no property fills are a place for computed values:

      #+COLUMNS: %ITEM(Task) %Effort(Effort) %START(Start) %END(End) %RESPONSIBLE(Who)
  #+BEGIN: columnview :exclude-tags (Skip)
  | Task   | Effort | Start            | End              | Who |
  | Task 1 | 1d     | <2021-03-13 Sat> | <2021-03-14 Sun> | Ian |
  | Task 2 | 3d     | <2021-03-15 Mon> | <2021-03-18 Thu> | Joe |
  #+END:
  #+TBLFM:@2$4..@>$4=date($3)+duration($2)

    The block has no separator under its header row (unless :hlines adds them), so a plain column formula ($4=...) would run on the header too; the range target starts at row 2 instead.

    On the server

    Org: orgs Update Dynamic Blocks and Org: orgs Update Dynamic Block at Cursor have the orgs server refresh the blocks instead (it saves the buffer first and the result comes back into it). The server has its own columnview implementation; see the orgs Server section.

    Dynamic Blocks

    Blocks that write themselves

    A dynamic block is a pair of lines whose contents are generated:

      #+BEGIN: NAME :param value :param value
  ...generated text...
  #+END:

    With the cursor on the #+BEGIN: line, alt+o c c (org_recalc, the do what I mean key) or Org Exec Dynamic Block (org_execute_dynamic_block) runs the writer called NAME with the parameters and replaces everything between the two lines with what it returns. Anything you typed inside the block is lost on the next run.

    OrgEverywhere has three writers built in and runs your own from Packages/User/orgdynamic/. The orgs server can refresh dynamic blocks too (see the end of this page).

    clocktable

    A table of the clocked time of the heading the block sits under and of every heading below it.

      #+BEGIN: clocktable :maxlevel 2
  | Heading   | Time |      |
  |-----------+------+------|
  | Project   | 5:30 |      |
  | \_ Design |      | 2:00 |
  | \_ Build  |      | 3:30 |
  #+END:
    Parameter Meaning
    :maxlevel N how many time columns, one per level (default and minimum 2); deeper headings are still listed
    :scope subtree the only scope supported: the current heading's subtree

    The times are the CLOCK: lines of the file as it is in the buffer. For clock reports across all your files use Org: orgs Clock Report (orgs Server section), or let the server refresh the block.

    columnview

    A table of headings and their properties. See Column View.

      #+BEGIN: columnview :id global :indent t :maxdepth 2
  #+END:

    insertdatetime

    Writes the current date and time; a small example of a writer.

      #+BEGIN: insertdatetime
  2021-03-09 20:55:12.345678
  #+END:

    Writing your own

    A writer is a python file in Packages/User/orgdynamic/; its file name is the block name. Packages/User/orgdynamic/greeting.py runs for #+BEGIN: greeting. It defines Execute(view, params), which returns the new contents of the block as a list of lines:

      import datetime

  def Execute(view, params):
      who = params.Get('who', 'world')
      return ["Hello " + who, "It is " + str(datetime.date.today())]
      #+BEGIN: greeting :who Ian
  Hello Ian
  It is 2021-03-09
  #+END:
    • view is the Sublime view of the org file.
    • params holds the :name value pairs of the #+BEGIN: line: params.Get(name, default), params.GetInt(name, default), params.GetList(name, default) (for (a b c) values).
    • The lines are indented to the level of the heading the block is in.
    • An optional PostExecute(view, params, region) runs after the text is in the buffer; the built in table writers use it to have the table aligned (view.run_command("table_editor_next_field")).

    This is the place for things that shell out: a ledger or beancount balance, a report from a build server, the output of a script.

    A file you change is reloaded the next time the block runs. The built in writers live in the package's orgdynamic folder; a user file with the same name takes their place.

    On the server

    Org: orgs Update Dynamic Blocks refreshes every dynamic block in the file on the orgs server, Org: orgs Update Dynamic Block at Cursor only the one under the cursor. The buffer is saved first and the server's result comes back into it. The server has its own writers (clocktable, columnview and more), which can see all your org files; see the orgs Server section. Your python writers in Packages/User/orgdynamic/ only run locally.

    Source Blocks

    Running code in org files, diagrams, tangling, and timesheets and gantt charts.

    Running Source Blocks

    Source blocks as live code

    A source block is code in an org file. In org mode (where the feature is called babel) a block can also be run, and what it prints is written back into the file under it. Notes, the code that produced a number and the number itself stay together: a lab notebook, a runbook, a report that refreshes itself.

      #+BEGIN_SRC python :var x=5
    print(str(x * 2))
  #+END_SRC

  #+RESULTS:
  : 10

    Put the cursor anywhere in the block and press alt+o c c (org_recalc, the do what I mean key; space c c with NeoVintageous) or run Org Exec Source Block (org_execute_source_block). The block's output replaces its #+RESULTS:, which is created if there is none.

    • Org Exec All Source Blocks runs every block in the file, from the bottom up.
    • The file has to exist on disk: an unsaved buffer is saved before a block runs. :file paths are relative to the org file.
    • Blocks run locally, in Sublime. The orgs server can run them instead; see the end of this page.

    See Babel: active code in org mode for the org side of the story.

    Languages

    Language Runs with Setting
    python Sublime's own python, inside the editor
    javascript, js node nodejsPath
    sh, bash bash (/bin/bash; wsl.exe on Windows) bashPath
    powershell Windows PowerShell (Windows only)
    cmd, bat cmd.exe (Windows only)
    perl perl perlPath
    csharp dotnet (experimental) dotnetPath
    gnuplot gnuplot gnuplot
    plantuml, graphviz, ditaa, mermaid the diagram tools; see Diagrams (see there)

    The paths are settings in OrgEverywhere.sublime-settings:

      "nodejsPath": "/usr/local/bin/node",
  "bashPath":   "/bin/bash",
  "perlPath":   "/usr/bin/perl",
    • python blocks run in Sublime's plugin host (python 3.8): no separate python is needed, only Sublime's modules can be imported, and the block can use view and window to script the editor. A block that loops forever freezes Sublime.
    • The other languages are written to a temporary file and run as a separate program. Their working directory is Sublime's Packages/User folder, not the org file's folder: use absolute paths in scripts.
    • builtinSourceBlockHandlers lists the languages that are loaded and builtinSourceBlockAliases maps other names onto them (bash to sh, js to javascript, bat to cmd).

    Header arguments

    Everything after the language on the #+BEGIN_SRC line is header arguments, :name value pairs. They can also be set for more than one block. From weakest to strongest:

    1. orgBabelDefaultHeaderArgs in the settings, the defaults for every block (:session none :results replace :exports default :cache no :noweb no).
    2. babel-args and babel-args-LANGUAGE in the settings, as strings of header arguments.

    3. #+PROPERTY: lines in the section the block is in:

        #+PROPERTY: header-args: :var y=11
  #+PROPERTY: header-args:python: :var z=12

      Note the colon after header-args and after the language.

    4. The heading's property drawer:

        :PROPERTIES:
  :header-args: :var g=global
  :header-args:python: :var x=5
  :var: v=10
  :END:
    5. A #+HEADER: line right above the block.
    6. The #+BEGIN_SRC line itself.

    Variables and inputs

    :var name=value hands a value to the block. The value can be

    • a number or a string,
    • the #+NAME: of a table: the block gets the rows (a list of lists in python, an array in javascript, …),
    • the #+NAME: of a list,
    • the #+NAME: of another source block: that block runs first and its result is the value (chaining).
      #+NAME: my-table
  | name  | value |
  | Hello | 25    |
  | World | 42    |

  #+BEGIN_SRC python :var DATA=my-table
    print(DATA)
  #+END_SRC

  #+RESULTS:
  : [['name', 'value'], ['Hello', 25], ['World', 42]]

    Chaining lets each step use the language that suits it: pull data with a shell script, reshape it in python, plot it with gnuplot.

      #+NAME: greeting
  #+BEGIN_SRC python
    print("hi")
  #+END_SRC

  #+BEGIN_SRC python :var x=greeting
    print(x + " there")
  #+END_SRC

    Results

    :results takes up to one word from each group:

    Group Words Default
    What is kept output, value output
    What it is verbatim, scalar, table, vector, list, file verbatim
    How it is wrapped raw, drawer, code, org, html, latex (none)
    Where it goes replace, append, prepend, silent replace
    • output is what the block prints. value is what it returns: the body is wrapped in a function, so python and javascript use return; for sh the value is the exit status.
    • verbatim puts each line behind : =. =table turns the output into an org table (a printed python list of lists, or comma, tab or space separated lines). list makes an org list. raw inserts the text as is.
    • drawer wraps the results in :results: / :end:; code, org, html and latex wrap them in a source block of that kind.
    • silent writes nothing into the file (the output goes to the console); append and prepend add to the existing results.
    • :file NAME writes the output into that file (relative to the org file) and puts a link to it into the results. Diagram languages make their picture there.
      #+NAME: in-table
  | a | b | c |
  | 1 | 2 | 3 |

  #+BEGIN_SRC python :var DATA=in-table :results value table
    return [[c * 10 for c in r] for r in DATA[1:]]
  #+END_SRC

  #+RESULTS:
  | 10 | 20 | 30 |

    Caching

    With :cache yes the results line carries a hash of the code (#+RESULTS[3f2a...]:). If the code has not changed since, the block is not run again and the stored results are used. Careful with blocks that have side effects or read changing data.

    Safety

    • :eval never or :eval no - the block never runs.
    • :eval query - you are asked each time.
    • :eval query-export - you are asked when the block runs as part of an export.

    Put :eval query into orgBabelDefaultHeaderArgs to be asked before any block runs.

    Calling a block

    The #+CALL line

    A named block is a function. #+CALL: runs it with other arguments and puts the results under the call:

      #+NAME: double
  #+BEGIN_SRC python :var x=1
    print(x * 2)
  #+END_SRC

    #+CALL: double(x=21)

    Run it with alt+o c c on the call line. The call line has to be indented, as it is in the body of a heading.

    Inline blocks

    A one liner inside a paragraph:

      The answer is src_python[:var x=21]{print(x*2)} {{{results(=42=)}}}

    alt+o c c on it, or Org Exec Inline Source Block, writes or replaces the results macro after it.

    From a table

    sbe(name, var=value) in a table formula runs a named block (here the double block above) and puts its result into the cell: tables feed blocks, and blocks feed tables.

      | from python |
  | 42          |
  #+TBLFM:@2$1=sbe('double',x=21)

    Org Show Source Tests opens the source block unit tests, which use sbe to check every language and diagram tool (you need those tools installed for their tests to pass).

    Noweb

    With :noweb yes a line <<name>> in a block is replaced by the code of the blocks named name (blocks with :noweb-ref name, or the block with #+NAME: name) before the block runs: literate programming's way of assembling a program from pieces.

      #+BEGIN_SRC python :noweb-ref print-it
    print("Hello World")
  #+END_SRC

  #+BEGIN_SRC python :noweb yes
    <<print-it>>
  #+END_SRC

    <<name(x=20)>> runs the named block with those arguments instead and pastes its output:

      #+BEGIN_SRC python :var x=10 :noweb-ref evalsource :results raw
    print("print('hi " + str(x) + "')")
  #+END_SRC

  #+BEGIN_SRC python :noweb yes
    <<evalsource(x=20)>>
  #+END_SRC

  #+RESULTS:
  : hi 20

    The <<...>> has to be on a line of its own. See Noweb reference syntax.

    Tangling

    Tangling writes the code of a file's blocks out as plain source files. Org Tangle File (org_tangle_file) takes every block with :tangle yes and writes it to a file next to the org file, named after it, with the language's extension: the python blocks of notes.org go to notes.py. Each file starts with a comment saying where it came from, and each block is preceded by a comment with its line number.

    The local tangler only knows :tangle yes: a file name as the value is not honoured. The orgs server's tangler follows org's rules: Org: orgs Tangle File writes each block to its :tangle file and understands :mkdirp, :shebang, :padline, :tangle-mode, :comments and noweb references.

      #+BEGIN_SRC python :tangle tools/report.py :mkdirp yes :shebang #!/usr/bin/env python3
    print("report")
  #+END_SRC

    Exporting

    :exports says what an export shows: code, results, both or none. default shows the code, except for the languages in htmlDefaultSkipSrc (plantuml, graphviz, ditaa, gnuplot), which show only their picture. The html exporter runs the file's blocks first (htmlExecuteSourceOnExport). See Exporting.

    Running blocks on the server

    The orgs server has its own babel. Org: orgs Execute Source Block runs the block (or #+CALL:) at the cursor there, Org: orgs Execute All Source Blocks every block of the file. The buffer is saved first and the server writes the results into the file, which comes back into the buffer. The server only runs code when babel.enable is set in its orgs.yaml; it has its own list of languages and sessions. See the orgs Server section.

    Adding a language

    A language is a python file. Put LANG.py in Packages/User/orgsrc/ and blocks of that language run through it; a file with the name of a built in language replaces it. The built in handlers in the package's orgsrc folder (sh.py, perl.py, powershell.py) are short and make good templates.

    Function Required Does
    Execute(cmd, sets) yes runs the code, returns the output as a list of lines
    Extension(cmd) the file extension: the code is written to a temporary file cmd.filename
    PreProcessSourceFile(cmd) rewrites cmd.source first, typically to declare the :var values
    WrapStart(cmd), WrapEnd(cmd) text put before / after the code
    LineCommentPrefix() the comment marker, used when tangling
    PostExecute(cmd) runs after the results are in the buffer
    GeneratesImages(cmd) true to show the images in the file afterwards

    cmd.source is the code, cmd.params the header arguments (cmd.params.Get('var', None)), cmd.sourcefile the org file and sets.Get(name, default) reads a setting. Shared handlers are welcome upstream.

    Diagrams

    Pictures from text

    A source block does not have to be a program. Blocks in a diagram language describe a picture; running the block (alt+o c c, or Org Exec Source Block) hands the text to the tool, writes the picture to the :file you name and links it under the block:

      #+BEGIN_SRC graphviz :file images/graph.png
    digraph G { a -> b; a -> c; c -> d }
  #+END_SRC

  #+RESULTS:
  [[file:images/graph.png]]

    • :file is relative to the org file. Always give one: without it the picture is written to diagram.png next to the org file and no link is made. plantuml and graphviz create a missing folder; for the other tools make the folder first.
    • The org file must be saved (it is saved for you before the block runs).
    • Afterwards the images of the file are shown inline. Org Show Images / Org Hide Images turn that on and off for the whole file, Org Show Image / Org Hide Image for the link under the cursor.

    The tools are not part of OrgEverywhere. Install the ones you want and give their paths in OrgEverywhere.sublime-settings. Restart Sublime after installing java or node, so that it sees the new PATH.

    When a file is exported to html the picture is shown and the diagram source is left out for the languages in htmlDefaultSkipSrc (plantuml, graphviz, ditaa, gnuplot by default); :exports on the block overrides that.

    PlantUML

    PlantUML draws sequence, class, state, activity and many more UML diagrams. It needs java on the PATH and plantuml.jar (brew install plantuml on macOS installs both).

      "plantuml": "/usr/local/Cellar/plantuml/1.2021.7/libexec/plantuml.jar",
      #+BEGIN_SRC plantuml :file images/plantuml1.png
    title Authentication Sequence

    Alice->Bob: Hello Request
    note right of Bob: Bob thinks about it
    Bob->Alice: Authentication Response
  #+END_SRC

    OrgEverywhere adds the @startuml and @enduml lines itself: leave them out of the block.

    Graphviz

    Graphviz lays out graphs and networks (brew install graphviz, or the download page). Point the setting at the dot program:

      "graphviz": "/usr/local/bin/dot",
      #+BEGIN_SRC graphviz :file images/graphviz.png
    digraph G {
      a -> b;
      a -> c;
      c -> d
    }
  #+END_SRC

    Argument Meaning
    :engine NAME another graphviz layout program (neato, circo, fdp, twopi…), found next to dot
    :fmt FORMAT the output format given to -T (png by default; svg, pdf, jpg…)

    Keep the extension of :file the same as :fmt.

    Ditaa

    Ditaa turns ascii art boxes and arrows into a picture. It is a java program: set the path to ditaa.jar (and java if java is not on the PATH).

      "ditaa": "/opt/ditaa/ditaa.jar",
  "java":  "/usr/bin/java",
      #+BEGIN_SRC ditaa :file images/ditaa.png
    +--------+       +----------+
    | Hello  | ----> | Hello2   |
    +--------+       +----------+
  #+END_SRC

    Ditaa always makes a png.

    Mermaid

    Mermaid draws flowcharts, sequence diagrams, gantt charts and more from a markdown like text. Install the command line tool with node (npm install -g @mermaid-js/mermaid-cli) and point the setting at mmdc (on Windows at mmdc.ps1, which is run through PowerShell):

      "mermaid": "/usr/local/bin/mmdc",
      #+BEGIN_SRC mermaid :file images/flow.png
    graph TD
      A[Start] --> B{Is it working?}
      B -- Yes --> C[Ship it]
      B -- No --> D[Debug] --> B
  #+END_SRC

    mermaid is not in htmlDefaultSkipSrc, so an html export shows its source as well as the picture unless the block says :exports results.

    gnuplot

    gnuplot blocks are plots written in gnuplot's own language:

      "gnuplot": "/usr/local/bin/gnuplot",
      #+BEGIN_SRC gnuplot :file images/sine.png
    set title "sin(x)"
    plot sin(x) with lines
  #+END_SRC

    The extension of :file picks gnuplot's terminal (png, jpg, gif, svg, ps, html for a canvas, txt for ascii art) and the matching set term / set output lines are added for you.

    A table given with :var DATA=table-name is meant to arrive as a gnuplot data block ($DATA) for plot "$DATA" using 1:2. In this release the table is not passed through to gnuplot blocks; to plot a table use Org Plot Table and a #+PLOT: line (see Tables), or put the data into the block.

    The orgs server

    The orgs server's babel (Org: orgs Execute Source Block) can run diagram blocks too when it has the tools, and among its exporters (Org: orgs Export File) are mermaid and gantt, which turn a whole org file into a diagram. See the orgs Server section.

    Timesheets and Gantt Charts

    Planning with properties

    A project plan is mostly already in your org files: the tasks are todo headings, and a few properties say how long each one takes, who does it and what it waits for. OrgEverywhere turns those into a timesheet table, a mermaid gantt chart or a Google Charts gantt page.

    Since 2.0 the tasks come from the orgs server: every todo and done heading of every file the server knows (archived trees and projects - tasks with sub tasks - left out), saved files only. The server must be connected.

    Where What it is
    SCHEDULED the start (else the deadline, else the first active timestamp)
    :EFFORT: the estimate (1d, 3h, 2d4h); the end is start plus effort
    :ASSIGNED: who does it
    :AFTER: the ID of the task it waits for
    :ORDERED: t on a parent: each child waits for the one before it
    :SECTION: a group name for the gantt chart (also read from the parent)
    CLOCK: lines the time spent, summed over the heading and its sub headings

    ASSIGNED and SECTION can also be set for a whole file with #+PROPERTY: ASSIGNED Ian above the first heading, and for every file with the timesheetDefaultAssigned and timesheetDefaultSection settings.

      * Website
    :PROPERTIES:
    :ORDERED:  t
    :SECTION:  Website
    :END:
  ** TODO Design
     SCHEDULED: <2021-03-15 Mon>
     :PROPERTIES:
     :EFFORT:   2d
     :ASSIGNED: Ian
     :ID:       design-task
     :END:
  ** TODO Build
     :PROPERTIES:
     :EFFORT:   4d
     :ASSIGNED: Joe
     :END:
  * TODO Launch party
    :PROPERTIES:
    :EFFORT:   1d
    :AFTER:    design-task
    :END:

    The timesheet table

    Org Timesheet Table (org_insert_timesheet) inserts a table of those tasks at the cursor:

      |Name           |Estimate    |Start           |End             |Dep|Assigned|Spent  |X|
  |-
  |Design         |2d          |<2021-03-15 Mon>|<2021-03-17 Wed>|   |Ian     |3:15:00| |
  |Build          |4d          |                |                |1  |Joe     |       | |
  |Launch party   |1d          |                |                |1  |        |       | |
    • Dep is the number of the task, in this list, that it waits for.
    • Spent is the clocked time, X marks done tasks.
    • Press tab in it to align it. It is an ordinary table from then on: add formulas, plot it, export it.

    Org Choose Timesheet Table (org_choose_timesheet) first asks for one of your AgendaCustomViews and uses that view's filters (tags, files, query…; see the Agenda guide) to choose the tasks; the plain command uses the Default view.

    Gantt charts

    Both chart commands ask for an AgendaCustomViews entry, like Org Choose Timesheet Table, and write into the folder named by the timesheetPath setting:

      "timesheetPath": "/Users/me/notes/schedule",
  "mermaidPath":   "/usr/local/bin/mmdc",
  "timesheetDefaultStartDate": "2023-01-02",
    • Org Timesheet Mermaid Gantt (org_generate_mermaid_gantt_chart) writes schedule.mermaid and renders it to project_schedule.png with the mermaid command line tool (mermaidPath; note this is not the mermaid setting the source blocks use). Tasks are grouped by SECTION, weekends are skipped, and a task without a date starts on timesheetDefaultStartDate. A one letter ASSIGNED value sets the bar's style: D done, A active, C critical, M milestone, X critical and done, Y critical and active. The render step runs on Windows and macOS only; on Linux run mmdc on schedule.mermaid yourself.
    • Org Timesheet Google Gantt (org_generate_google_gantt_chart) writes project_schedule.html, a page that draws the chart with Google Charts in the browser (it needs internet access). Bars are coloured by who is assigned; done tasks are 100% complete.

    Gantt charts on the server

    The orgs server draws gantt charts of its own:

    • Org: orgs Open Web UI, then Gantt Chart, shows an interactive chart of your tasks in the browser.
    • Org: orgs Export File with the gantt exporter turns the current file into a gantt chart page, and mermaid into a mermaid file.

    See the orgs Server section.

    Doing it by hand

    For a one off chart, a column view block plus a little formula gives a plan table you can adjust by hand (see Column View):

      #+COLUMNS: %ITEM(Task) %Effort(Effort) %START(Start) %END(End) %RESPONSIBLE(Who)
  #+BEGIN: columnview :exclude-tags (Skip)
  | Task   | Effort | Start            | End              | Who |
  | Task 1 | 1d     | <2021-03-13 Sat> | <2021-03-14 Sun> | Ian |
  | Task 2 | 3d     | <2021-03-15 Mon> | <2021-03-18 Thu> | Joe |
  #+END:
  #+TBLFM:@2$4..@>$4=date($3)+duration($2)

    This follows the Gantt charts in org video, which goes on to plot such a table with gnuplot.

    Exporting

    Turning org files into html, pdf through latex, other formats through pandoc, and slides.

    Exporting Overview

    From org to everything else

    Org is a document format as much as a planning tool: an org file can become a web page, a pdf, a slide deck or a word document. OrgEverywhere can export in two ways:

    • Built in exporters that run inside Sublime on the buffer: html, LaTeX / pdf and reveal.js slides, plus pandoc for everything pandoc can write.
    • The orgs server's exporters: html with themes, LaTeX and pdf, markdown, reveal.js and other slide formats, mermaid, gantt charts and whatever else the server is configured with. They need the server.
    Command Writes Guide
    Org Export File As Html file.html Html Exporter
    Org Export Subtree As Html file_subtree.html Html Exporter
    Org Export File As Latex file.tex LaTeX Exporter
    Org Export File As Pdf file.tex and file.pdf LaTeX Exporter
    Org Export File As Reveal Js file.html (slides) Reveal.js
    Org Pandoc File To Html file.html Pandoc
    Org Pandoc Subtree To Html file.html Pandoc
    Org: orgs Export File depends on the exporter below
    Org: orgs Export File as PDF file.pdf below

    The output goes next to the org file, with its name. Several built in exporters write file.html, so a reveal.js export replaces an html export of the same file and the other way round.

    What the built in exporters read

    The html, LaTeX and reveal.js exporters share one reader. A few things to know:

    • The document is the headings and their text. Text above the first heading is not exported; the keywords there (#+TITLE:, #+AUTHOR:, #+DATE:, #+EMAIL:, #+LANGUAGE:, #+HTML_STYLE:, #+LATEX_CLASS:, #+REVEAL_THEME:…) are read as the file's options.
    • Keywords that act where they stand (#+SETUPFILE:, #+LATEX_HEADER:, #+HTML:, #+CAPTION:, #+ATTR_HTML:, #+ATTR_LATEX:) work inside a heading.
    • Write keywords in upper case.
    • Most file options have a setting of the same meaning, used when the file does not say: #+HTML_STYLE: and HtmlStyle, #+LATEX_CLASS: and latexClass, #+REVEAL_THEME: and RevealTheme.
    • #+SETUPFILE: path reads the lines of another file in its place: a way to share a header between documents.
    • Drawers, planning lines (SCHEDULED:, DEADLINE:, CLOCK:), #+TBLFM: and other org bookkeeping lines are left out.
    Source blocks and results

    :exports on a source block decides what an export shows: code (the default), results, both or none. The diagram languages in htmlDefaultSkipSrc (plantuml, graphviz, ditaa, gnuplot) show only their results unless the block says otherwise. See Running Source Blocks.

    An export can run the file's source blocks first, so results are fresh:

    Exporter Setting Default
    html htmlExecuteSourceOnExport true
    LaTeX latexExecuteSourceOnExport false
    reveal.js revealExecuteSourceOnExport false

    Blocks marked :eval query-export ask first.

    Images

    A link to a .png, .jpg, .gif or .svg file becomes a picture. The file is looked for

    1. at the path in the link (absolute, or relative to the org file),
    2. in the folders of the imageSearchPath setting,
    3. in an images folder in each of your orgDirs (used for this only; the server decides which files are org files).

    The orgs server's exporters

    Org: orgs Export File (org_orgs_export) lists the exporters the server has (server.exporters in its orgs.yaml), and for html and slide exporters the themes it has; pick one and the result is written next to the org file. Org: orgs Export File as PDF goes straight to a pdf (the server needs LaTeX).

    • The buffer is saved and the server reads that before exporting.
    • Slide decks are written as file.revealjs.html (and so on), so they do not replace an html export.
    • orgsExportOpen says what happens afterwards: "ask" (default), "always" opens the result (html and pdf in the browser, the rest in Sublime), "never".

    The server's exporters understand more of org than the built in ones (#+INCLUDE, footnotes, export settings) and give the same result as the orgs command line and the web ui. See the orgs Server section for the exporters and their themes.

    Which one to use

    • Quick html of your notes, styled your way: the built in html exporter.
    • A pdf: Org: orgs Export File as PDF, or the built in LaTeX exporter if you have LaTeX locally and want to tweak the .tex.
    • Slides: the built in reveal.js exporter, or the server's reveal.js, impress.js and other slide exporters.
    • Word, epub, markdown and the rest: pandoc, or the server's markdown exporter.

    Html Exporter

    Exporting a file to html

    Org Export File As Html (org_export_file_org_html) writes the org file as file.html next to it: one self contained page with the style inlined. Org Export Subtree As Html (org_export_subtree_as_org_html) exports only the heading under the cursor, as file_subtree.html.

    Before exporting, every source block of the file is run so that its results are current; turn that off with htmlExecuteSourceOnExport: false.

    The page has

    • the title, author and language of the file (#+TITLE:, #+AUTHOR:, #+LANGUAGE:),
    • each heading as a section whose heading can be clicked to fold it,
    • code coloured by highlight.js (loaded from a CDN),
    • checkboxes as html checkboxes (a partly done [-] shows checked; set htmlExportPartialCheckboxChecked: false for unchecked),
    • a footer with the date, the author and when it was made.

    For the general rules (what is read from where, images, source block results) see Exporting.

    Styles

    The look comes from a style: a set of files named after it. Choose the style per file or for every file:

      #+HTML_STYLE: funky
      "HtmlStyle": "funky",

    OrgEverywhere comes with blocky (the default), funky, plain and refined. A style is up to four files:

    File Goes
    STYLE.css into a <style> in the head: most of the look
    STYLE_inheader.html into the head: fonts, scripts, meta tags
    STYLE_heading.html at the top of the body: a banner, a logo
    STYLE_footing.html at the end of the body: a rule and a footer line

    OrgEverywhere looks for them in Packages/User/htmlstyles/ first, then in the package's own htmlstyles folder. To make a style of your own, copy the files of a built in one into Packages/User/htmlstyles/ under a new name and change them. A _inheader.html that loads fonts:

      <link href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Bebas+Neue&family=Montserrat&display=swap" rel="stylesheet">
    Adding to a style

    Four more options add to whatever the style has. Each can be a file keyword or a setting; the value is either the text itself (anything with a < or { in it) or the path of a file to read.

    Mind the spelling: for these four the file keyword is written in mixed case and the setting in upper case (the other way round from #+HTML_STYLE: / HtmlStyle):

    Keyword Setting Adds to
    #+HtmlCss: HTML_CSS the css
    #+HtmlInHeader: HTML_INHEADER the head
    #+HtmlHeading: HTML_HEADING the top of the body
    #+HtmlFooting: HTML_FOOTING the end of the body 
      #+HtmlCss: body { max-width: 50em; }
  #+HtmlHeading: /Users/me/notes/banner.html

    Html in the document

    • #+HTML: <hr class"fancy">= puts a line of html into the page.
    • A #+BEGIN_EXPORT http … #+END_EXPORT block is copied into the page as is. Note the language: the html exporter passes http export blocks through (and drops html ones).
    • An html comment line <!-- NAME attributes --> before an image link adds those attributes to the <img> of the next image whose path contains NAME. (#+ATTR_HTML: is not applied to images.)
    • #+CAPTION: A caption above a table gives it a numbered caption (Table 1: …).
    • A property drawer's properties become attributes of the heading's <section>: :class: warning gives <section class"warning">=, for styling single sections.
    • #+BEGIN_NOTES blocks become <aside class"notes">=.
      * Results
    :PROPERTIES:
    :class: highlight
    :END:
    <!-- throughput width="600" style="border: 1px solid #ccc" -->
    [[file:images/throughput.png]]

    #+CAPTION: Throughput by week
    | week | jobs |
    |------+------|
    |    1 |  120 |

    Diagrams and code

    Diagram blocks (plantuml, graphviz, ditaa, gnuplot; the htmlDefaultSkipSrc setting) show only their picture; other blocks show their code. :exports on a block overrides both: code, results, both, none.

    The server's html

    Org: orgs Export File with the html exporter renders the file with the orgs server's html exporter and lets you pick one of its themes. It is the same html the orgs command line and web ui produce; see Exporting and the orgs Server section.

    Pandoc's html

    Org Pandoc File To Html converts with pandoc instead; see Pandoc.

    LaTeX Exporter

    LaTeX and pdf

    LaTeX is a typesetting system; its most common output is a pdf. OrgEverywhere's LaTeX exporter turns an org file into a .tex file and, if you have LaTeX installed, into a pdf.

    • Org Export File As Latex (org_export_file_as_latex) writes file.tex next to the org file. No LaTeX installation is needed for this.
    • Org Export File As Pdf (org_export_file_as_pdf) writes file.tex and runs pdflatex on it in the org file's folder, giving file.pdf.

    No LaTeX? Org: orgs Export File as PDF has the orgs server make the pdf (the server needs LaTeX instead); see Exporting.

    Installing LaTeX

    A LaTeX installation is large; give it some time.

    • Windows: TeX Live or MiKTeX.
    • macOS: MacTeX (brew install --cask mactex).
    • Linux: TeX Live from your distribution (texlive-latex-extra).
    • More: Getting LaTeX.

    Then tell OrgEverywhere where pdflatex is:

      "latex2Pdf": "/Library/TeX/texbin/pdflatex",

    The pdf command runs pdflatex once. LaTeX needs a second run to fill in the table of contents and references: export again (or run pdflatex by hand) when they are empty.

    The preamble loads listings, hyperref, graphicx, longtable, wrapfig, rotating, amsmath, amssymb, ulem, babel (greek, english), CJKutf8 and a few more, so a full installation (or those packages) is needed.

    Document options

    Keyword Setting Meaning
    #+TITLE: \title
    #+AUTHOR: \author
    #+DATE: \date
    #+LATEX_CLASS: latexClass the document class (article by default)
    #+LATEX_HEADER: a line added to the preamble
    #+OPTIONS: toc:nil, toc:2, title:nil, author:nil, date:nil

    #+LATEX_CLASS: and #+OPTIONS: go at the top of the file. #+LATEX_HEADER: lines (like the other line keywords) are only read inside a heading: put them in the first section.

      #+TITLE: Field Report
  #+AUTHOR: Ian
  #+LATEX_CLASS: report
  #+OPTIONS: toc:2

  * Introduction
    #+LATEX_HEADER: \usepackage{geometry}
    #+LATEX_HEADER: \geometry{margin=2cm}
    ...

    Headings become \section, \subsection, \subsubsection, \paragraph and \subparagraph.

    LaTeX in the document

    • #+LATEX: \newpage puts a line of LaTeX into the document.
    • @@\vspace{1em}@@ puts LaTeX inline.
    • #+BEGIN_EXPORT latex … #+END_EXPORT is copied as is.
    • Math: $x^2$ and \(x^2\) inline, \[ ... \] displayed.
    • <<target>> becomes a \label; *target* a \hyperref to it.

    Pictures and tables

    An image link becomes \includegraphics; by default at 80% of the line width. #+ATTR_LATEX: above it sets the size, #+CAPTION: turns it into a figure:

      #+CAPTION: The pipeline
  #+ATTR_LATEX: :width 0.5\linewidth :placement [h]
  [[file:images/pipeline.png]]
    Attribute For Meaning
    :width, :height, :scale images \includegraphics options
    :float tables t, multicolumn, sideways, wrap or nil
    :placement tables, figures [h], [!htp]… (a figure needs a caption)
    :center nil tables, figures do not centre
    :environment tables tabular (default), longtable, tabularx…
    :mode tables math or inline-math for a matrix
    :caption tables, figures a caption (instead of #+CAPTION:)

    A table with a caption floats as a table. Image folders are added to \graphicspath; images are found as described in Exporting.

    Source blocks

    Source blocks become lstlisting environments of the listings package, with the block's language. When a language name in org is not the one listings knows, map it:

      "latexListingPackageLang": {
      "python": "Python",
      "lua":    "[5.2]Lua",
  },

    :exports results or none on a block leaves its code out. Blocks are not run before a LaTeX export unless latexExecuteSourceOnExport is true.

    On the server

    The orgs server's latex exporter (Org: orgs Export File) and its pdf export (Org: orgs Export File as PDF) are an alternative that needs no local LaTeX; the server also has a dnd exporter for documents in the style of the D&D 5e books. See Exporting and the orgs Server section.

    Pandoc

    Installing pandoc

    Pandoc converts between document formats and reads org files. It is the way to Word, OpenDocument, EPUB, reStructuredText, MediaWiki and the many other formats OrgEverywhere has no exporter for.

    Install it from pandoc.org (brew install pandoc, apt install pandoc, or the Windows installer) and give its path:

      "PandocPath": "/usr/local/bin/pandoc",

    Html through pandoc

    Org Pandoc File To Html (org_export_file_as_html) runs

      pandoc -s -c <style>.css [-H <style>_inheader.html] -o file.html file.org

    on the saved org file (save first: unsaved changes are not seen) and writes file.html next to it.

    The style is chosen by the PandocStyle setting (blocky by default); its .css and _inheader.html are taken from the pandoc folder of the OrgEverywhere package. The css is linked, not copied into the page, so the page only looks right on the machine that made it. For a page to share, prefer the built in html exporter (Html Exporter), which inlines its style.

    Org Pandoc Subtree To Html is meant to do the same for the heading under the cursor; in this release it fails before running pandoc, so export the subtree with the built in Org Export Subtree As Html instead.

    Other formats

    For anything else run pandoc yourself, from a terminal or a build system:

      pandoc notes.org -o notes.docx
  pandoc notes.org -o notes.epub
  pandoc notes.org -t rst -o notes.rst

    A pdf goes through LaTeX. A few useful options:

      pandoc --pdf-engine=xelatex notes.org -o notes.pdf
  pandoc --pdf-engine=xelatex -V CJKmainfont="KaiTi" notes.org -o notes.pdf
  pandoc --pdf-engine=xelatex --highlight-style zenburn notes.org -o notes.pdf
  pandoc --pdf-engine=xelatex --toc -N notes.org -o notes.pdf
    • -V CJKmainfont=... picks a font with Chinese, Japanese and Korean characters.
    • --highlight-style colours code (pandoc --list-highlight-styles lists them).
    • --toc -N adds a numbered table of contents.

    See Markdown to pdf with pandoc for more.

    Pandoc on the server

    The orgs server can run pandoc too: with its pandoc exporter configured (and pandoc installed where the server runs), Org: orgs Export File offers it and writes the format the server is set up to produce. See the orgs Server section.

    Reveal.js Slides

    Slides from an outline

    reveal.js presentations are web pages: they run in any browser, need no presentation software and can be put on a web server. Org Export File As Reveal Js (org_export_file_reveal_js) turns an org outline into one:

    • each top level heading is a slide,
    • its sub headings are slides stacked below it (reveal.js's vertical slides: press down to go through them),
    • the text under a heading is the slide's content: lists, tables, code, images, links.

    The result is file.html next to the org file; it loads reveal.js (4.1) from a CDN, so presenting needs internet access unless you host reveal.js yourself (REVEAL_LOCATION below). Note that the html exporter writes the same file name: export the deck last, or keep it in a file of its own.

    This exporter is simpler than emacs' org-reveal, but covers what a talk usually needs.

      #+TITLE: Our Quarter
  #+REVEAL_THEME: night
  #+REVEAL_TRANS: slide

  * Where we are
    - Shipped the importer
    - Halved the build time
  * The numbers
    | Month | Builds | Minutes |
    |-------+--------+---------|
    | Jan   |    410 |      12 |
    | Feb   |    455 |       6 |
  ** By team
     ...

    Options

    Each option is a keyword at the top of the file or a setting for every deck.

    Keyword Setting Default Values
    #+REVEAL_THEME: RevealTheme league black, white, league, beige, sky, night, serif, simple, solarized, moon, blood
    #+REVEAL_HIGHLIGHT: RevealHighlight zenburn the code colouring: zenburn, monokai
    #+REVEAL_TRANS: RevealTransition none none, fade, slide, convex, concave, zoom
    #+REVEAL_TRANS_SPEED: RevealTransitionSpeed default default, fast, slow
    #+REVEAL_CSS: RevealCss css added to the page
    #+REVEAL_LOCATION: RevealLocation jsdelivr where reveal.js is loaded from (a url ending in /)

    The search, zoom, notes, math and markdown plugins are loaded.

    Per slide settings

    Properties on a heading set that slide's background and transition:

      * Thank you
    :PROPERTIES:
    :reveal_background: images/crowd.jpg
    :reveal_background_size: cover
    :reveal_background_opacity: 0.4
    :reveal_trans: zoom
    :END:
    Property reveal.js attribute
    reveal_background, reveal_background_image data-background-image
    reveal_background_size data-background-size
    reveal_background_position data-background-position
    reveal_background_repeat data-background-repeat
    reveal_background_opacity data-background-opacity
    reveal_background_color data-background-color
    reveal_background_trans data-background-transition
    reveal_background_video data-background-video
    reveal_background_video_loop data-background-video-loop
    reveal_background_video_muted data-background-video-muted
    reveal_trans data-transition
    reveal_trans_speed data-transition-speed

    See the reveal.js documentation on backgrounds and transitions for the values.

    Speaker notes and code

    A #+BEGIN_NOTES … #+END_NOTES block is the slide's speaker notes: press s during the talk to open the speaker view.

    Source blocks are shown with their code coloured. reveal.js's code options go on the #+BEGIN_SRC line:

      #+BEGIN_SRC python :data-line-numbers 2-3 :data-trim
    def greet(name):
        message = "Hello " + name
        print(message)
  #+END_SRC
    • :data-line-numbers turns on line numbers; a range (2-3, 1,4-5) highlights those lines.
    • :data-trim removes the surrounding blank space, :data-noescape passes html in the code through.

    Source blocks are not run before export unless revealExecuteSourceOnExport is true. Languages listed in revealDefaultSkipSrc (as well as those in htmlDefaultSkipSrc) show only their results.

    Slides from the server
